One warm brand hue, a warm-leaning neutral ramp and four semantic colours. Token names are identical in light and dark — only the values swap. Saturated colour is reserved for status badges and primary actions; every other surface is neutral.

The blocks — styles/tokens.css, imported once before Tailwind
:root {
  /* brand */
  --brand-50:  #FEF4F0;  --brand-500: #D85B32;
  --brand-100: #FDE4DB;  --brand-600: #B8431F;
  --brand-200: #FAC7B6;  --brand-700: #93351A;
  --brand-300: #F3A184;  --brand-800: #6E2814;
  --brand-400: #E87B54;  --brand-900: #4A1B0E;

  /* neutral */
  --n-0:   #FFFFFF;  --n-500: #7C7A75;
  --n-50:  #FAFAF9;  --n-600: #5C5A55;
  --n-100: #F4F4F2;  --n-700: #44423E;
  --n-200: #E7E6E3;  --n-800: #2C2B28;
  --n-300: #D3D2CE;  --n-900: #1C1B19;
  --n-400: #A8A6A1;  --n-950: #121110;

  /* roles */
  --bg-base:        var(--n-50);
  --surface:        var(--n-0);
  --surface-raised: var(--n-100);
  --surface-sunken: var(--n-200);
  --border:         var(--n-200);
  --border-strong:  var(--n-300);
  --text:           var(--n-900);
  --text-muted:     var(--n-600);
  --text-subtle:    var(--n-500);
  --accent:         var(--brand-600);
  --accent-hover:   var(--brand-700);
  --accent-on:      var(--n-0);
  --accent-subtle:  var(--brand-50);
  --focus-ring:     var(--brand-600);

  /* semantic */
  --success: #15803D; --success-subtle: #ECFDF3;
  --success-border: #A7E8C0; --success-text: #14532D;
  --warning: #B45309; --warning-subtle: #FFF7E6;
  --warning-border: #F5D58A; --warning-text: #78350F;
  --danger:  #C22B2B; --danger-subtle:  #FEF0F0;
  --danger-border:  #F3B4B4; --danger-text:  #7F1D1D;
  --info:    #1D5FB8; --info-subtle:    #EEF4FD;
  --info-border:    #B3CCF0; --info-text:    #14355F;

  /* radii */
  --r-sm: 4px; --r-md: 8px; --r-lg: 12px;
  --r-xl: 16px; --r-full: 999px;

  /* shadows */
  --sh-sm:    0 1px 2px rgba(28,27,25,.06);
  --sh-md:    0 2px 6px rgba(28,27,25,.08);
  --sh-lg:    0 8px 24px rgba(28,27,25,.12);
  --sh-sheet: 0 -4px 20px rgba(28,27,25,.14);

  /* spacing */
  --sp-1: 4px;  --sp-2: 8px;  --sp-3: 12px;
  --sp-4: 16px; --sp-5: 20px; --sp-6: 24px;
  --sp-8: 32px; --sp-10: 40px; --sp-12: 48px;
  --sp-16: 64px;

  /* z */
  --z-base: 0;  --z-sticky: 10; --z-nav: 20;
  --z-dropdown: 30; --z-overlay: 40;
  --z-modal: 50; --z-toast: 60;
}
[data-theme="dark"] {
  /* the ramps do not change — only the roles */

  --bg-base:        var(--n-950);
  --surface:        var(--n-900);
  --surface-raised: var(--n-800);
  --surface-sunken: var(--n-950);
  --border:         #3A3835;
  --border-strong:  #55534E;
  --text:           var(--n-100);
  --text-muted:     var(--n-400);
  --text-subtle:    var(--n-500);

  /* the brand lightens so it stays legible on
     near-black and keeps 4.5:1 with dark text */
  --accent:         var(--brand-400);
  --accent-hover:   var(--brand-300);
  --accent-on:      #2A1008;
  --accent-subtle:  #2E1409;
  --focus-ring:     var(--brand-300);

  --success: #4ADE80; --success-subtle: #10281A;
  --success-border: #1E5637; --success-text: #A7E8C0;
  --warning: #FBBF3C; --warning-subtle: #2A1D08;
  --warning-border: #6B4A12; --warning-text: #F5D58A;
  --danger:  #F87171; --danger-subtle:  #2C1212;
  --danger-border:  #6E2626; --danger-text:  #F3B4B4;
  --info:    #7FB0F2; --info-subtle:    #101E31;
  --info-border:    #24476F; --info-text:    #B3CCF0;

  /* shadows carry less on dark: raise alpha and
     always pair with a --border hairline */
  --sh-sm:    0 1px 2px rgba(0,0,0,.40);
  --sh-md:    0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.50);
  --sh-lg:    0 8px 28px rgba(0,0,0,.60);
  --sh-sheet: 0 -4px 24px rgba(0,0,0,.65);
}

/* Tailwind reads them, so utilities stay tokenised:
   theme.extend.colors = {
     surface: 'var(--surface)',
     accent:  'var(--accent)', … }
   → class="bg-surface text-accent"          */

/* Theme is an attribute on <html>, set by a
   ThemeService before first paint. No class
   toggling per component, no second stylesheet. */
02 · Typography & density Typography.dc.html 1440 × 1900 px
02 · Foundations

Typography & density

Plus Jakarta Sans throughout, at two densities. One codebase, two body sizes: compact 13px carries back-office tables, comfortable 16px carries customer and driver content. Density is an attribute on the shell, not a per-component prop.

Family
Plus Jakarta Sans
Humanist geometric: rounder than Inter, with a tall x-height that survives 13px table rows and a distinctive a, g and 1 that keep 400/500/600/700/800 telling each other apart at small sizes.
Fallback stack: 'Plus Jakarta Sans', ui-sans-serif, system-ui, sans-serif
Regular 400
Medium 500
Semibold 600
Bold 700
Extrabold 800
Numerals
Every price, quantity, order id and countdown sets font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums so digits hold their column when a value ticks. Proportional figures stay on prose only.

Customer & driver

Focus is always visible
A 2 px ring in --focus-ring with a 2 px offset in the surface colour, drawn with box-shadow so it clears the border and never shifts layout. Never outline: none without a replacement; :focus-visible, so a pointer click does not ring.
Loading keeps its width
The label stays in the DOM at visibility: hidden and the spinner is absolutely centred, so the button does not resize and the row below does not jump. The button is disabled and aria-busy="true" while it spins.
Sizes by role
lg 56 is the phone primary, full width in the thumb zone. md 40 is the default everywhere. sm 32 is back-office only — pointer input, so it may drop under the 44 px touch floor. An icon-only button is square at its size and carries an aria-label.
04 · Inputs Inputs.dc.html 1440 × 2120 px
04 · Components

Inputs

Every field is a real <label for> plus a real control — never a styled div. Controls are 44 px tall at comfortable density, 32 px in the back office. Hint text is always present in the layout so an error does not push the form down when it appears.

Errors appear only after touch
A control validates on blur, not on keystroke. Until the user has left the field, the form shows no red — a half-typed phone number is not an error yet. In Angular terms: show the message when control.invalid && (control.touched || form.submitted).

Surfaces

Containers are neutral: --surface with a 1 px --border and, where elevation is real, one shadow step. No tinted card backgrounds, no accent left-borders. The mobile equivalent of a dialog is a bottom sheet — the same component with a different presentation.

Card

Trattoria Nono

Italian · Belgrade
See the menu
The whole card is not a link — the title and the action are. That keeps text selectable and gives the screen reader one target per destination.
Modal — confirm dialog

Cancel order #10482?

Trattoria Nono hasn’t accepted it yet. If it was paid by card, the hold is released — nothing is charged.

Focus is trapped and returns to the trigger on close; Escape closes; the scrim sits at --z-overlay, the dialog at --z-modal. The destructive verb is on the button, never just “OK”.
Bottom sheet — the mobile equivalent

Cancel this order?

The restaurant hasn’t accepted it yet. Nothing will be charged.

Same dialog semantics, presented from the bottom edge so both buttons land in the thumb zone. Drag handle is decorative; the sheet also closes on scrim tap and Escape.

Arrow keys move between tabs, Tab moves into the panel. Selection is carried by weight and the underline, not colour alone.

06 · Feedback Feedback.dc.html 1440 × 1900 px
06 · Components

Feedback

Four ways the app talks back: a toast for something that just happened, a spinner for a wait under a second, a skeleton for a wait the user can see the shape of, and a full-surface state when there is nothing or something broke. Never a spinner where a skeleton fits.

Toasts — desktop stack, bottom right
Order #10482 accepted
Moved to the kitchen lane.
Couldn’t change availability
Pljeskavica is back to Available. Your menu is unchanged.
Menu changes are live
Customers see the new prices from now on.
Stacked newest at the bottom, maximum three; a fourth replaces the oldest. Success and info auto-dismiss after 5 s, error never does. role="status" for the first two, role="alert" for the error, so a screen reader interrupts only when it matters.
Phone — above the nav
Your orders

Green Bowl

Order number copied

On a phone the toast sits above the bottom nav, never over it, full width minus 12 px, with one optional inline action.
Spinner
16 inline
24 button
36 panel
Placing your order…
Blocking waits always say what they are waiting for.
720 ms per turn, a 270° arc in --accent. Only for waits with no known shape — a payment, a submit. Under 300 ms nothing is shown at all, so a fast response does not flash.
Skeletons — shaped like the content that replaces them
Each skeleton matches the real block’s box: same heights, same gaps, same number of lines. Text lines vary in width so the page does not read as a barcode. Pulse is opacity 1 → 0.45 over 1600 ms, never a sweeping gradient.

Exactly as many skeleton rows as the page size, so the table does not grow when data lands. The wrapper carries aria-busy="true"; the bars themselves are aria-hidden.
Empty state
Nothing waiting
Orders appear here the moment they are placed. The dashboard updates on its own — nothing to do.
Icon, one sentence of what this place is for, and an action only when there is a genuinely useful one. Never an illustration that says nothing, never an exclamation mark.
Error state with retry
Could not load orders
The server did not respond. Your data is safe — nothing was lost. This usually clears within a minute.
ref 4f21c8a0 · 19:11:43
Says what failed, what it means for the user’s data, and offers the retry as the primary action. The reference is the response’s X-Correlation-Id, copyable, so support can find the request in Seq — no stack traces on screen.
07 · Motion & accessibility MotionA11y.dc.html 1440 × 1860 px
07 · Foundations

Motion & accessibility

The whole motion inventory is four transitions. Anything not on this list does not animate — no page transitions, no hover lifts, no parallax. Every entry has a prefers-reduced-motion fallback that keeps the information and drops the movement.

Transition
Duration
Easing
What moves
Reduced-motion fallback
Status change
160 ms
cubic-bezier(0,0,.2,1)
ease-out
A badge crossfades to the new label and rises 2 px. The row it sits in never reflows — badge width is set by its longest label.
Instant swap, no fade, no rise. The new label is what carries the change anyway.
Toast entry
220 ms in
160 ms out
cubic-bezier(.22,1,.36,1)
out: ease-in
Slides 12 px from the edge it is docked to and fades in. Stack members shift with the same curve when one leaves.
Fade only, 100 ms, no slide and no stack shuffle. Dismiss timers are unchanged.
Driver marker
900 ms
linear
matches the ping interval
Tweens between GPS pings so the map reads as movement, not teleporting. Linear only — an eased tween implies acceleration that did not happen.
The marker jumps to each new fix. The “last seen” time updates either way, so nothing is lost.
Skeleton pulse
1600 ms
infinite
ease-in-out
opacity 1 → .45
Opacity only. No sweeping gradient — a moving highlight across a full table is the single most nauseating thing a loading state can do.
Animation off, bars held at 0.7 opacity. Still clearly placeholders.
/* durations and curves are tokens too */
:root {
  --dur-status: 160ms;
  --dur-toast-in: 220ms;
  --dur-toast-out: 160ms;
  --dur-marker: 900ms;
  --dur-pulse: 1600ms;
  --ease-out:    cubic-bezier(0, 0, .2, 1);
  --ease-spring: cubic-bezier(.22, 1, .36, 1);
}

/* one global opt-out, not a per-component check */
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) {
  *, *::before, *::after {
    animation-duration: 1ms !important;
    animation-iteration-count: 1 !important;
    transition-duration: 1ms !important;
    scroll-behavior: auto !important;
  }
  .skeleton { animation: none !important; opacity: .7; }
  .spinner  { animation-duration: 2000ms !important; }
  .marker   { transition: none !important; }
}
Status is never colour alone
Every badge carries an icon and a word. The colour is the third signal, not the first — the same row read in greyscale still tells a colour-blind manager which orders need attention.
In colour

Icons are stroked, 13 px, currentColor, and aria-hidden — the word beside them is what a screen reader announces. A status change also fires a polite live-region update.

Dark is why --accent moves to brand-400 and the semantics to their light tints: brand-600 on near-black reaches only 2,9:1. Button text on those fills is --accent-on, a near-black derived from the hue, not pure white.
Keyboard
Every interactive thing is a real control, so Tab order is DOM order. Dialogs and sheets trap focus and return it to the trigger. The back-office table supports arrow-key row movement with a roving tabindex, and a “Skip to orders” link is the first focusable element on every screen.
Announcements
One polite live region per screen for status changes and toasts; role="alert" only for errors the user must act on. A countdown is not announced every second — it updates silently and announces at the 5 and 1 minute marks.
Targets & zoom
44×44 px minimum on customer and driver screens, 8 px between neighbours. Layouts hold at 200% browser zoom and at the largest OS text size without clipping — which is why no fixed-height row carries two lines of text.

08 · Components

Status legend

Every enum the backend can send, in both themes. One badge component, five tones, and a rule that decides the tone from the meaning of the state — not from the vocabulary it belongs to. Every badge carries a label, and an icon beside it; colour is never the only carrier.

The tone rule — read the state, then pick the tone; never the other way round
Neutral
Waiting. Nobody has acted yet, and nobody needs to act right now.
Pending
Info
In progress. The system or a person is working on it, and it is moving.
Preparing
Success
It ended, and it ended well. Terminal, or the last good step before terminal.
Delivered
Warning
Needs attention. Not broken yet, but a human has to do something.
Unassigned
Danger
Failed, rejected or cancelled. Terminal, and not the outcome anyone wanted.
Cancelled
Order status
OrderStatus
Six REST steps forward, two ways out, plus one the socket adds. Pending waits on the restaurant and arrives on the socket as "Placed"; the dashed DriverAssigned exists only on the socket — on a cold load it comes from the delivery being Assigned; everything between Accepted and OutForDelivery is motion; Delivered is the only good terminal.

Badge pairing — an order always shows two badges: where the food is, and where the money is

The cause reads left to right: the charge failed, so the order was cancelled. Two reds, one story.
#4830

Pending Cash on delivery
Two neutrals. Cash owes nothing to the payment system, so it never turns green — it goes NotRequired and stays quiet.
Why the pair never contradicts itself
The two badges answer different questions — where is the food and where is the money — so they are never two opinions about one thing. The state machine also forbids the combinations that would read as a contradiction: payment reaches Captured only on the transition into Delivered, and a Failed authorisation always drives the order to Cancelled in the same transaction. Green beside red cannot occur.
The legal pairs, in full
PendingNotRequired · Authorizing
Accepted → OutFor…NotRequired · Authorized
DeliveredCaptured · NotRequired (cash collected)
RejectedReleased · NotRequired
CancelledReleased · Failed · NotRequired
Anything outside this table is a bug, not a state — the UI shows the raw enum names and a support link rather than inventing a tone for it.
Colour is never the only signal
Every badge carries its label, and a glyph whose shape differs per tone: a clock for waiting, an arrow or spinner for motion, a tick for success, a triangle for attention, a crossed circle for failure. Desaturate the sheet and the states are still distinguishable — which is also how they read to the 8% of male users with a red–green deficiency. Badge text sits at 4.5:1 or better on its own fill in both themes; the fills are tints, never the saturated --success / --danger hues, which are reserved for 1px borders, dots and icon strokes.

The compact top bar
52 px, position: sticky; top: 0, --z-sticky, one hairline border and --sh-sm once the content scrolls under it. It holds context on the left (address, or screen title) and at most two controls on the right. No back button on a tab root; a pushed screen swaps the left slot for one.
Tabs and the safe area
Four tabs, each a 48 px target in a 60 px bar. The bar's padding is calc(6px + env(safe-area-inset-bottom)), so on a device with a home indicator the row lifts instead of sitting under it, and on a device without one the term resolves to 0 and nothing shifts. Scroll containers add the same value so the last card clears the bar.
The cart count
A 17 px pill on the cart glyph, --accent with a 2 px ring in the bar's own background so it reads on both themes. It shows 1–99, then 99+. It is announced, not just drawn: the tab's accessible name is “Cart, 3 items”. At zero the badge is removed from the DOM rather than hidden.
Why the driver app is bare
A driver is holding a phone at a doorway, often one-handed, often in the rain. There is no tab bar because there is nothing to switch to: the shell is a status strip and whatever the current job needs. Actions are 56 px, the primary one is the widest thing on screen, and history and profile live behind the menu rather than competing with the job. There are no earnings anywhere: the platform has no driver pay model.

Sidebar, expanded and collapsed
248 px expanded, 64 px collapsed, and the collapse is a user preference stored per account — not a viewport rule, so a manager who prefers the rail keeps it on a 27″ screen. Items keep their icons in both states, so the collapse changes width, not vocabulary. In the rail the label becomes the button's accessible name and a tooltip; counts shrink to a dot-sized pill on the glyph.
Sections, not a flat list
Groups are labelled (Platform, Provisioning, Support for an administrator; Orders, Menu, Restaurant for a manager) and a group appears only when one of the user’s roles unlocks an item inside it — roles come from GET users/me and are mapped to items client-side, so an agent never sees an empty Provisioning heading. Section order is fixed across users so muscle memory survives a role change.
The top bar's four jobs
Left: which area you are in. There is no global search — no endpoint searches across orders, drivers or tickets. Right: whether the app is live, what happened while you were looking away, and who you are signed in as. Nothing else earns a place — page-level actions belong in the content well beside the heading they act on.
768 and below
The rail stays, the labelled sidebar becomes an overlay over a scrim, and the top bar drops the connection pill for a bare dot with an accessible name. Tables become cards: a 6-column grid at 1440 is unreadable at 768, and horizontal scrolling inside a table is worse than stacking.
11 · Role nav Navigation.dc.html 2200 × 1680 px
11 · Navigation

Role-driven navigation

The client is told which roles a person holds and nothing finer: GET users/me returns roles, the access token carries none, and permissions are resolved on the server per request. So the navigation is built from roles through one client-side manifest — and it is a courtesy, never a control. A menu item the client shows wrongly costs a 403, not a breach.

What the client receives
GET users/me  →  200
{
  "userId":    "6f1c…",
  "email":     "ana.t@example.com",
  "firstName": "Ana",
  "lastName":  "Todorović",
  "roles":     ["SupportAgent",
                "Administrator"]
}
No permissions field, and none in the token. userId is the module-side id — the one orders, tickets and socket groups use — not the token’s sub. A 404 here means the account was deactivated: the client logs out.
Role names are exactly Customer, RestaurantManager, DeliveryDriver, SupportAgent, Administrator — a union type, not a string.
How the tree is built
1
Every nav item in the manifest declares roles — the roles whose seeded permissions let it work. The list is a copy of the backend’s permission table, kept in one file.
2
An item renders when the user holds any of its roles. No match, no item — never a greyed-out row that only tells people what they lack.
3
A section renders when one of its items does; an area joins the switcher when one of its sections does. One area resolved → the switcher is a plain label with no chevron.
4
roleGuard reads the same manifest, so a pasted deep link to a hidden page lands on the friendly 403 from sheet 59 instead of an empty screen.
5
Finer controls inside a page — Approve, Assign to someone else — hide behind hasRole('Administrator'), the only proxy available, and let the server’s answer be the real gate.

You hold 2 roles. Switching changes what you see, not what you can do.
Both areas sit in one sidebar divided by a rule; the switcher jumps and sets the landing page. Live activity appears because Ana is a SupportAgent — as an Administrator alone she would not receive its socket frames.
Areas are views, not accounts
Switching area is not switching user: no re-authentication, no session change, no loss of what you were doing. It is a filter over one shell, restorable from the URL, so a link Ana sends opens the same page for anyone whose roles allow it.
After login, a home per role
The landing route is picked from roles in a fixed order — Administrator, SupportAgent, RestaurantManager, DeliveryDriver, Customer — so a person with two roles lands on the more operational one. A role-less account (an empty array is possible) gets a plain “this account has no access yet” page and a log-out.
When roles change mid-session
Nothing pushes a role change to the client — no socket frame carries it. The server applies it on the very next request, so the first sign is a 403 on a control that is still visible. The client answers with the 403 toast, re-reads /me, rebuilds the tree and moves to the first permitted page; a 404 from /me logs out.
12 · Connection state Connection.dc.html 1800 × 1560 px
12 · Realtime

Connection state

The app holds exactly one authenticated WebSocket. On connect — and on every reconnect — it re-reads authoritative state over HTTP and only then applies socket deltas, because anything that arrived while the socket was down is simply gone. The indicator exists to tell the user which of those two worlds they are looking at: live, or a snapshot.

Connected
live
Desktop top bar
Connected
Mobile top bar
Live
The quietest state gets the quietest treatment: a neutral pill with a green dot, no animation, no colour on the fill. It is there so that its absence is noticeable — a user who glances at it and sees green has an answer without reading a word. On mobile it shrinks to “Live”; below 768 px it becomes the dot alone, with the state in its accessible name.
Reconnecting
stale
Desktop top bar
Reconnecting…
Mobile top bar
Reconnecting
Amber, because something needs attention but nothing is broken yet. The glyph rotates once per 1.2 s and stops under prefers-reduced-motion, where the pill pulses its border opacity instead. Retries back off 1s, 2s, 4s… to 30 s; the pill does not count them down, because a user cannot act on the number.
Offline
frozen
Desktop top bar
Offline
Mobile top bar
Offline
Reached after roughly 30 s of failed retries, or immediately when the browser reports the network is gone. Red, static, and paired with the banner below — but still only a pill in the corner. No modal, no full-screen takeover: a manager reading the last known state of twelve orders is doing something useful, and a dialog would take it away.
The stale banner — under the top bar, not over the content
Live orders
Reconnecting…
Live updates paused. Showing the state as of 14:02:11.
#4821
Kod Gazde
OutForDelivery
#4824
Pizzeria Mimo
ReadyForPickup
The rows stay legible and interactive — they are not dimmed, because dimming would suggest they are wrong rather than old. What changes is the promise: the banner names the exact moment the data was true, and write actions that depend on fresh state (Accept, Mark ready, Claim) become disabled with the reason on hover and in their accessible description.
Reconnect: re-read, then apply deltas
1
Socket drops
The indicator goes amber immediately. Deltas that arrive after this point are dropped, not queued — the client cannot know what it missed.
2
Backoff retries
1s, 2s, 4s … capped at 30 s, with jitter so a restarted gateway is not hit by every client at once. After ~30 s the pill turns red.
3
Socket opens, authenticated
Incoming deltas are buffered in memory. Nothing is applied to the UI yet — applying a delta to a stale snapshot is how a cancelled order reappears as active.
4
Re-read authoritative state over HTTP
Every open view refetches its own query. The banner stays up and its text changes to “Catching up…”; rows are replaced in place rather than cleared to skeletons, so the table never flashes empty.
5
Drain the buffer, resume live
Buffered deltas are applied in order on top of the fresh snapshot, the banner dismisses itself, and the pill goes green. A row whose status changed while the user was away animates once, over 200 ms, so the change is noticed rather than silently swapped.
Subtle, and never in the way
The indicator lives in the top bar in both shells and never moves. It has no dismiss control, because it is a state, not a message. The only escalation above a pill is the banner, and the only escalation above the banner is disabling the specific actions that would be unsafe — never a blocking dialog.
What a driver sees
The driver app is the one place offline is loud, because a driver acting on a stale job can deliver to the wrong door. The status strip takes the full width in red, and Mark delivered is replaced by “Waiting for signal — your last action is saved and will send automatically”. Driver actions are the only ones queued rather than dropped: picked up and delivered replay in order on reconnect, and a 409 on replay means the first attempt already landed — treated as success, not as an error. Location pings are never queued; a stale position is worse than none.
Announced, not just drawn
The pill is an aria-live="polite" region: going offline and coming back each announce once, in words. The banner is role="status" and takes focus only if the user tabs to it. No state is carried by the dot's colour alone — the label is always present, and at the smallest size it moves into the accessible name.
13 · Notifications Notifications.dc.html 1800 × 1560 px
13 · Realtime

Notification bell & panel

The feed is built entirely from socket events received while this tab has been open. There is no notification history endpoint, so there is nothing to page back through and nothing to restore after a refresh. The design's job is to be honest about that rather than to imitate an inbox it cannot back up.

The bell
none
4 unread
capped
none
4 unread
capped
The count is unread-in-this-session, nothing more. It never animates or bounces; a socket event that matters enough to interrupt gets a toast instead, and the bell just accumulates. Opening the panel marks everything visible as read and the badge disappears — there is no server to sync that to, so it cannot come back.
Which events reach the bell
OrderStatusChangedcustomer — into Accepted, DriverAssigned, OutForDelivery, Delivered, Rejected or Cancelled
RestaurantActivitymanager — a new "Placed" order (also chimes), and Cancelled
SupportActivityagent — Rejected and Cancelled only; everything else is the feed on sheet 48
DeliveryOfferednever the bell — it takes the driver’s whole screen (sheet 37)
DriverLocationChangednever — it moves the map and nothing else
Those are the only five frames the hub sends — there is no ticket, refund or payment frame, so none of those can reach the bell. Every other delta updates the screen silently. A feed that lists each Preparing → ReadyForPickup transition is a log, and nobody reads a log.

Session-scoped, stated in the UI
Both the populated panel and the empty state name the moment the session began and say the list is not stored. That one sentence is what stops the bell from being read as an inbox — and it is cheaper than building a history API to satisfy an expectation the design itself created.
What a reconnect does to it
Nothing is invented for the gap. After a reconnect the feed gains a divider reading “Offline 14:02–14:05 — events during this time were not received”, so the sequence stays truthful. The lists themselves are correct, because they were refetched over HTTP.
Read is local, and that is fine
With no server state there is nothing to sync, so “read” means “read in this tab”. Two tabs keep two counts. Rather than hide that, the panel caps at the 50 most recent entries and drops the oldest — a bounded list nobody relies on beats an unbounded one people half-trust.
Keyboard and screen reader
The bell is a real <button> with aria-expanded and an accessible name that carries the count in words. The panel is a focus-trapped menu dismissed by Escape, each entry a link to the thing it is about. Unread is marked by a dot and a tinted row and heavier type, never by tint alone.

None of the following exist in the data model, so none of them appear on this screen. Adding any one of them is a backend change first and a design change second:
Search Cuisine filters Near me Distance sorting Open now Ratings Delivery time Delivery fee Logos Cover photos Promotions Favourites
The row is text-only for the same reason: the only image URL anywhere in the model hangs off a menu item. A card built for a photo that never arrives is a grey box with a name under it — worse than a clean list of names. So the list leans on typography and generous row height instead of pretending to be a gallery.
Load more, not infinite scroll
With only page and pageSize there is no total count to show, so the button says nothing it cannot prove — no “20 of 63”, no progress bar. It simply disappears when a page comes back with fewer rows than pageSize, which is the one reliable signal that the list has ended.
Infinite scroll was rejected: it makes the bottom tab bar the only fixed ground on the screen, it hides the end of a short list behind a spinner that never resolves, and on a flaky connection it retries silently. A button that the user pressed has an obvious failure state — it goes back to being a button.
While a page loads
The rows already on screen stay put; only the button changes. A failed page restores the button and drops an inline error above it — the list is never thrown away because page 3 failed.
Active is silence
Both states are in the data, but only one is worth ink. Badging every healthy row green would put five identical badges on one screen and train people to ignore the sixth, which is the one that matters.

Loading
restaurant + menu in one request
The item row, with and without a photo
Text is the constant and the photo is the variant — not the other way round. Name, description and price sit in a left column that owns the row's width; an optional 76 px square hangs on the right. A row without a photo simply ends sooner, with no gap, no placeholder frame and no change in height rules. That is why the list still looks composed when a whole category has no photos, which is the likely case.
The add control overlaps the photo's bottom edge by 14 px so it stays at the row's right margin whether or not a photo is there, and it is 44 px either way. On a real build the grey square is an <img> with object-fit: cover; here it is a labelled placeholder rather than a stock photo, so nobody mistakes a mock for a decision.
Sold out reads three ways
The row keeps its place in the menu — removing it would make a category look shorter than the restaurant intended and lose the customer's landmark. Instead: a neutral Sold out badge beside the name, every text colour stepped back one notch, and the add button disabled with a minus glyph rather than a plus. Tapping it does nothing and announces “Ćevapi, sold out”.
Neutral, not red: the item is not an error and nothing failed. Red here would sit next to genuine payment failures elsewhere in the product and cheapen them. The row is dimmed but still legible at 4.5:1 — a customer should be able to read what they are missing and decide to come back.
Stepper in place of the plus
Zero is a single 44 px plus button. One tap turns that same slot into a − / n / + stepper, the row's border picks up the accent, and the quantity uses tabular figures so it does not jitter between 9 and 10. Going back to zero collapses the stepper to the plus — there is no separate delete affordance to learn on this screen.
Each press is optimistic and local; the cart is client state until the order is placed, so there is no spinner on a stepper and no way for a slow network to make a tap feel lost.
The tab bar gives way
This is the one customer screen where the four bottom tabs are replaced — by the cart bar, full width, in the thumb zone, carrying count and running subtotal. A menu is a task, not a place, and the back arrow already returns to Home. Two competing bars at the bottom of a 375 px screen would leave the primary action fighting for attention with navigation the customer is not using yet.
With an empty cart the bar is absent rather than disabled, so the menu gains 68 px of list.

One number, and it is the last thing on the screen
There is no delivery fee, tax line, tip, service charge, promo field or grand total, because the order model holds a subtotal and a commission rate and nothing else. The commission is taken from the restaurant's side and never shown to the customer.
That makes the footer unusually easy: one label, one figure, one button. The figure is set at 22 px/800 rather than the 15 px a subtotal would normally get in a stack of five money rows — with nothing below it to be summed into, the subtotal is what the customer pays, and it should carry that weight. Tabular figures throughout, so the column stays aligned as quantities change.
Worth naming as a risk: a customer who has used other delivery apps may look for the fee they expect and wonder what is missing. The honest fix is one line of copy under the subtotal — but only once someone can say authoritatively what the customer is and is not charged. Inventing that sentence here would be worse than leaving the number bare.
Sheet on the phone, panel on the desktop
Same component, two presentations. The sheet rises over a scrim, caps at 90% height so the menu stays visible behind it, and puts Place order within 56 px of the bottom edge — squarely in the thumb zone, and the only accent-filled element on screen. It is dismissed by the handle, the close button, a downward drag or the scrim.
The desktop panel is docked, not floating: at 1440 px there is room for the cart to sit beside the menu permanently, so adding an item has a visible destination and no dialog interrupts the browse. It scrolls its own line items with the subtotal and button pinned to its base.
Going to zero deletes the line
At quantity 1 the minus becomes a bin glyph in --danger — the same control, warning that the next press removes the line rather than showing a 0. There is no confirm dialog for one line item: it is cheap to undo by pressing plus again, and a modal for every removed side order would be exhausting. The whole-cart wipe on sheet 17 does get a dialog, because that one is not cheap to undo.

Why the confirm isn’t red
Emptying the cart is a side effect, not the goal — the customer is trying to order a pizza. Painting their intended action red teaches people that red means “the thing I wanted”, which is exactly the lesson that makes a genuinely dangerous red button get clicked through elsewhere. The warning lives in the amber icon, the named consequence and the itemised list; the button stays the accent and says plainly what it does.
Both buttons name their outcome
Not “OK” and “Cancel” — with two destructive-sounding paths, Cancel is genuinely ambiguous (cancel the add, or cancel the cart?). Each label carries its restaurant name, so the choice can be read without re-reading the paragraph above it. The list of what disappears is shown rather than counted: “3 items” is abstract, Mešano meso is not.
Order of the buttons
On the phone the primary sits on top, inside the thumb arc, with the safe choice beneath it — a 56 px target at the bottom edge is the easiest thing to hit, and the customer got here by deliberately tapping add. On the desktop the pair is right-aligned with the primary last, following the platform’s reading order. Escape and the scrim both resolve to keep the cart; focus opens on the safe button and returns to the add control that opened the dialog.

Don’t close the app — this takes a few seconds.
Errors wait to be earned
A field validates on blur, never on the first keystroke — nobody should be told “postal code is invalid” while typing the first digit of a valid one. Once a field has been touched and failed, it then re-validates as you type, so the error clears the moment the input becomes correct rather than waiting for another blur.
Pressing Place order touches every field at once, so a customer who taps straight through sees everything that is missing in one pass, and focus moves to the first failing field. The message says what good looks like — “Serbian postal codes have 5 digits” — not that the value is wrong.
The error is red text and a red border and a glyph and aria-invalid with aria-describedby pointing at the message. Optional fields say “optional” in the label rather than marking the other six with asterisks.
Double-submit protection, three layers
1
The button goes disabled on the first press and stays that way until the request settles. It does not un-disable on a slow network.
2
The form behind it is disabled and dimmed, so nothing can change under a request that is already in the air.
3
The request carries an idempotency key generated when the checkout screen opened. A retry — by the user, the network layer or a background refresh — returns the same order instead of creating a second one. This is the layer that actually matters; the other two are courtesy.
The button keeps its own width and height while loading, so nothing reflows. Its label changes to a statement of what is happening, not a bare spinner — “Placing your order…” tells a customer on a stalled connection that the press registered. The glyph spins once per 1.2 s and holds still under prefers-reduced-motion.
Payment is a choice of two, so it is two radios
Not a dropdown, not a segmented control, not a “payment method” sub-screen — with two options and a selected default, everything is visible and one tap away. The card row says what actually happens to the money (authorised now, charged on delivery), because the difference between an authorisation and a charge is exactly what a customer will call support about.
The whole row is the label, so the 375 px target is 58 px tall rather than a 20 px radio dot. Selection is carried by the accent border and the filled radio together, never by border colour alone.
Pin my location adds coordinates, nothing else
There is no geocoder, so the button cannot fill in a street. What it can do is attach latitude and longitude to the delivery address — optional fields, and the ones the Delivery service uses to find a nearby driver and draw the drop-off pin. Once set it reads “Location pinned · remove”. If the browser denies permission the button returns to rest with one inline line; the order still places, it just tracks less well. The typed address is always what the driver reads.

Checkout failure — card declined

POST orders succeeds at once; authorisation happens afterwards. A few seconds later the payment moves Authorizing → Failed and the order goes to Cancelled with it — so this is the order-detail screen in that state, reached from checkout, not a checkout error. There is no path back from a terminal state, which means there is no retry to offer — only a new order. The screen’s whole job is to say that plainly and make the next order one tap away.

There is no “Retry payment”
The order reached Cancelled alongside the failed authorisation, and terminal means terminal — no endpoint will revive it. A retry button would have to quietly create a different order under the same heading, which is how a customer ends up with two dinners and no idea why. So the buttons say order again, and the new order gets a new number.
The cart is the recovery
For a card order the cart is kept until the payment reaches Authorized (a cash order clears it at once), so after a decline both buttons lead back to a checkout that is already filled in — same restaurant, same items, same address. The primary switches payment to cash because that is the one route that cannot be declined again; the secondary keeps card and opens the payment method. Whichever they pick, it is one screen to a placed order, not a rebuild.
Say what is known, and stop
The platform is told that authorisation failed, not why — issuers do not share that. So the copy does not guess at insufficient funds, expiry or fraud checks, and it does not tell the customer to call their bank as if the problem were theirs. It states the outcome, states that nothing was charged (the sentence people actually want), and moves on. The declined order still appears in the order list as Cancelled · Payment failed, so nothing disappears from history.
20 · Item changed CheckoutChanged.dc.html 1840 × 1520 px
20 · Customer

Checkout failure — item changed

The cart is client state; prices and availability are not. The server prices every line from its own menu and refuses only an item that is no longer available (Orders.MenuItemNotAvailable) — a price change it would simply charge. So Place order first re-reads the menu (one cached GET) and diffs it against the cart; if anything moved, this sheet opens instead of the request. No order exists yet, so this is recoverable — but only the customer can approve a new number, so the screen shows exactly what changed and waits.

Per line, with the old value still visible
A single “prices have changed” banner over the whole cart would force the customer to audit every row themselves. Instead each affected line gets its own block naming the item, the nature of the change and both numbers — old struck through, new in bold — and the unchanged lines are collapsed into one quiet group so the diff is the screen.
A price rise and a removal read differently
A rise is amber with an up arrow — it costs the customer money and deserves the attention tone. A sold-out line is neutral with a struck-through name: nothing failed, and the subtotal went down. Note that both can land at once, and the net change can be either direction, which is why the footer shows the old subtotal beside the new rather than a “+/−” badge that would be wrong half the time.
Never re-price silently
The primary button carries the word accept and sits under the new figure, so the press is consent to that number and not just impatience. If every line in the cart has gone unavailable there is nothing to accept: the sheet becomes a plain message and a single Back to the menu, because an empty accepted order is not a thing the model can hold. And the re-check runs again on the next submit — the menu can move twice. If the server still refuses an item after the pre-flight (a race), the same sheet opens with that line marked sold out.

What “active” means
Not a flag — a derived set: every order whose status is not Delivered, Rejected or Cancelled. When a socket event moves the last active order into a terminal state it crosses the divider into Earlier, and if the Active group empties the heading goes with it. No “0 active” label, no placeholder card.
Active cards are visibly heavier — accent border, larger type, a chevron and the placed time spelled out — because they are the reason anyone opens this screen. History rows keep the same anatomy one step quieter, so the eye can still scan a column of badges.
Two badges, always both
Even when the payment badge is unexciting. Pending · Cash on delivery tells a customer the restaurant has not answered yet and that nothing will be charged — two facts they would otherwise have to open the order to learn. The pairing rules from sheet 08 hold here; the customer-facing labels use sentence case (“Out for delivery”) while the enum names stay in the back office.
No reorder button
There is no endpoint that clones a past order, and faking one client-side would break on the first sold-out item or changed price — landing the customer in sheet 20 from a button that promised one tap. A past order row leads to its detail; ordering the same food again starts at the restaurant, like any other order.

Three timeline states, no fourth
Done — filled accent dot with a tick, label at 600, a real timestamp where the backend keeps one. Current — hollow ring with a centre dot, label at 800 and a step larger, timestamp in accent. Upcoming — hollow grey dot, muted label and no time at all: an estimate the backend cannot produce would be a promise the kitchen never made.
The connector above a reached step is accent, above an unreached one grey, so the filled length reads as progress without a separate bar. The current step is also the only one that may carry a sentence under it — on Pending that sentence does the work an ETA would otherwise be asked to do.
Cancel exists only where the machine allows it
The button renders in Pending and Accepted and is absent everywhere else — not disabled, absent. Once food is being cooked the customer's cancel is a conversation with the restaurant, and a greyed button with a tooltip would only teach them to keep pressing it. If a socket event moves the order to Preparing while this screen is open, the button and its footer disappear in the same render.
The dialog is red on both sides of the choice — a red confirm and an explicit Keep it — because here the destructive act is the goal, and the thing being destroyed is not cheap to rebuild. That is the opposite call to sheet 17, and deliberately so: the test is whether one press can be undone by another.
The driver arrives with the assignment
No driver card until delivery status reaches Assigned — no skeleton, no “finding a driver…” placeholder, because dispatch may take one second or ten minutes and a spinner that long reads as broken. When it appears it carries the name, the vehicle type and nothing else — that is everything the model holds, and there is no phone number to call. There is no message thread, so none is drawn.

A banner, because it is not a step
Drawing Rejected as a red sixth dot would put it on the same line as Preparing and Out for delivery — implying the order is somewhere along a route it left. The banner sits above the timeline, in the reading position the outcome deserves, and carries the tone, the explanation and both badges together.
The timeline underneath is retitled What happened and keeps only the steps that occurred, with the terminal event as its last row. The unreached steps are removed, not greyed: a greyed Delivered on a cancelled order reads as something still pending.
The pairing carries the money story
Rejected · Released — red then neutral. The order failed; the money did not. The authorisation was let go, which is an ordinary ending, so the payment badge stays neutral and the banner spells out that the hold was released.
Cancelled · Payment failed — red then red, and the cause reads left to right: the charge failed, so the order was cancelled. Two reds, one story, exactly as the pairing panel on sheet 08 promised.
Inside the banner both badges sit on a white fill rather than the banner's own pink, so the neutral one does not get read as red by proximity.
Say where the money went, first
Both banners put “nothing was charged” in bold in the second sentence, because that is the question a customer has before any other, and the one that otherwise becomes a support ticket. Neither invents a reason the backend does not hold: the restaurant gives a reason when it rejects, but the order the customer reads does not carry it (and the terminal step has no timestamp on the REST model either), and an issuer does not say why it declined.
Both screens keep the full items list and the address — a terminal order is still a record, and hiding what was in it makes the row in history useless. The single action at the bottom goes back to browsing; there is no reorder, so there is nothing else to offer.

Designed for the worst case it will actually meet: one hand, on a street, in direct sun, on a phone at half brightness. So the map is the screen, everything readable sits on an opaque card, targets are 56 px, and there is exactly one control floating over the map. No ETA, by decision
There is no ETA prediction in this platform — no routing service, no historical timings, nothing on any DTO or frame that carries an estimate. So the card has no slot for one: not a placeholder, not a dash, not a reserved gap. An empty “ETA —” on a screenshot reads as an unfinished feature, and an invented “about 20 minutes” would be the most complained-about string in the product.
What the customer gets instead is honest motion: the current step, how long it has been the current step, and the marker itself. If prediction is ever built it earns its own design pass then.
Built for sunlight and one thumb
Nothing legible is drawn on the map. Every label sits on an opaque white chip with a real border, because translucent overlays are the first thing to disappear at 50% brightness against pale tiles. Body text on the card is --text, not --text-muted — the usual grey caption fails outdoors even though it passes on a desk.
One target is 56 px and sits in the lower right where a right thumb rests: re-centre, floating clear of the card. There is no call button — the delivery carries the driver’s name and nothing to dial. The card itself never scrolls — everything on it is reachable without a second hand.
Markers are shape-and-colour, each with a white halo ring so they hold against any tile: dark dot for the restaurant, accent dot for the address, blue puck for the driver. There is no route line: no routing service exists, and a straight line between pins would read as the road.
No frame is not a frame at 0,0
Until the first position arrives there is no driver marker at all — not a grey one, not one parked on the restaurant, and certainly not one in the Gulf of Guinea. The map shows the two pins it genuinely knows, and the card says in plain words that the driver has not shared a location yet and what that means.
The re-centre control is also absent in this state: there is nothing to centre on. It appears with the marker.
Stale: freeze, label, then re-read
On disconnect the marker stops where it was, loses its fill for a dashed outline, and picks up a chip naming the time of the last frame. Nothing is extrapolated — a marker that keeps gliding on a dead socket is the one failure that actively misleads someone standing at a door.
Recovery follows the rule from sheet 12: on reconnect the client re-reads the order over HTTP first, applies the buffered deltas on top, then resumes live frames. So the marker may jump once, to where the driver actually is — that jump is correct and is preceded by the banner clearing. Position frames that arrived while the socket was down are simply gone; only the latest matters.

The card number never passes through this application — Stripe Elements collects it inside this page, in Stripe’s own iframes, and the platform never sees it. The card never touches this app
The fields are Stripe Elements: iframes Stripe renders inside our page, drawn here inside a dashed boundary so nobody on the team mistakes them for components we own. The flow is three calls — POST payments/payment-methods/setup-intents for a client secret, stripe.confirmCardSetup in the browser, then waiting for the webhook. We never receive a PAN or a CVC, which is what keeps the platform in PCI SAQ-A.
That is worth saying to the customer too, twice and plainly: a green strip naming Stripe above the fields, and a sentence underneath. It is the one place in the product where a security claim is both true and load-bearing — people abandon card forms they do not trust.
One card at a time is the platform’s rule: GET payments/payment-methods returns at most one, and saving another replaces it. So the screen says “your card” and offers Replace, never a list with Add — and the form says out loud which card it will replace.
Pending is a real state, so it gets a real row
Stripe confirms by webhook, so a card does not exist the moment the form is submitted — the endpoint itself says to poll rather than assume. Rather than pretend — optimistically drawing a card that might never arrive, or spinning a full-screen loader over a list that is perfectly readable — the pending card gets its own amber row above the card that is still current.
The copy tells the customer the one thing that saves them waiting: you can leave this screen. Polling continues in the background; on confirmation the amber row is replaced in place by the real card, which is the only animation on the screen. Replace card is disabled while one is pending, because two in flight cannot be told apart.
Polling backs off — 2s, 4s, 8s to 30s — and gives up after two minutes, replacing the row with “We didn’t hear back from Stripe” and a Try again. A row that spins forever is worse than an honest failure.
Four facts, and one derived
Brand, last four, expiry, added date — in that order of prominence, because the last four is how a person recognises their own card. Expiry is the only figure the UI may reason about: a card whose month has passed can carry a neutral Expired badge and drop out of the checkout picker without any new endpoint.
Removal is confirmed because it is not recoverable from this side — re-adding means the Stripe form again. The dialog names the card by its last four and says what is not affected, since “will this cancel my order?” is the fear behind the hesitation. Checkout may still offer Card for a moment after removal — Orders learns of it eventually — and an order placed in that window fails gracefully into sheet 19.

If something goes wrong with an order — a missing item, a payment you don’t recognise — open a ticket and we’ll look into it.
Internal notes are filtered server-side
The agent view in sheet 40 and this thread are the same ticket, but the customer endpoint returns only messages marked customer-visible. That filter lives on the server — in SQL — and the client adds one more line: any message whose visibility is InternalNote is dropped before rendering, never styled differently. Not a v-if over CSS — a note excluded by CSS is a note one screenshot away from a complaint, and this client should never receive text it must not show.
Nor does the customer see priority, assignee, escalation or category changes. Agents rename categories and bump priority as they triage; a customer watching Normal become Urgent would read it as alarm, and watching it go the other way as neglect.
Status is the one internal fact worth sharing
It answers the only question a waiting customer has: is anyone holding this? Open is amber, In progress blue, Resolved green, Closed neutral — the same tones as everywhere else in the product. Escalated is the exception: it is shown to the customer as In progress, because internally it means “this needs a senior agent” and to a customer it reads as “something has gone badly wrong”.
The composer stays open on a Resolved ticket so a customer can say “that didn’t fix it” without opening a second one. Whether the server accepts that reply is the ticket’s call; if it refuses, the composer is replaced by its detail line and a New ticket button. There is no live update: a reply shows up when the thread is re-read (it polls every ~20 s while open), and the backend emails the customer on every agent reply anyway.
Messages, not chat
Bubbles because the alternation is what matters, but none of the live-chat furniture: no typing indicator, no read receipts, no presence dot. There is no agent sitting there waiting, and the design should not imply one — the first reply here came seven minutes later, which is a good result, not a failure of a chat.
Agent messages are signed with the first word of authorName and “from Support” — or just “Support” when the name is null — and the customer’s own messages read “You”, because authorName is null for them by design. Refund workflow steps are agent-side; the customer hears about money from the agent, in words.

Two entry points, one form
Get help on the order detail opens this with the order pre-filled; New ticket on the tickets list (sheet 26) opens it empty. The order is optional by contract — not every problem is about an order — so it is a removable chip, not a required field.
POST support/tickets { orderId?, subject, category } returns the ticket id; the screen goes straight to that ticket’s thread so the customer writes the details where the agent will answer them.
Seven categories as a radio group
category is a fixed seven-value enum, sent by name (ItemMissing). On a phone that is a list of full-width radio rows — one tab stop, arrow keys between them, labels in the customer’s words rather than the enum’s. This is where the accessible-radiogroup exercise lives in the plan.
Nothing is pre-selected: the category is the customer’s first real decision, and a default would be accepted unread.
What is not here
No attachments or photos — there is no upload endpoint anywhere. No priority picker: priority is the agent’s call and the customer never sees it. No chatbot: Feature 3.1 was never built. An agent cannot open a ticket on a customer’s behalf (only an administrator can), so there is no agent version of this screen.

There is no profile API
Nothing on this tab is editable, because nothing here can be written anywhere. Name, email and roles come from GET users/me — the access token itself carries none of them — and there is no endpoint that would accept a change. Every row that would normally live on a settings screen is absent for the same reason:
Change password Edit name or email Saved addresses Preferences Email notifications Push notifications Language Theme Delete account Avatar upload
A greyed-out Change password would be worse than its absence: it promises a feature and blames the user for not having it. If any of these are wanted, each is a backend change first — and the delivery address that checkout collects per order is the one that should be questioned first, since customers will assume it is remembered.
Roles, shown because they explain the app
A customer sees one quiet chip. Someone who also holds a staff role sees both, and that is the honest place to surface it — the area switcher in sheet 11 is built from these roles, and this is where a person can check which hats the system thinks they are wearing. The chips are neutral: a role is a fact, not a status.
The avatar is initials from firstName and lastName, in the brand tint. There is no upload, so there is no camera badge hovering over it suggesting otherwise.
Log out, with no confirm
Outlined in --danger rather than filled: it is the most consequential control on the screen but not one anyone should be nudged toward, and it is the only destructive action in the product that costs nothing to undo — signing back in restores everything, because nothing lives on the device. So no dialog.
It sits below a spacer that pushes it to the bottom of the scroll area rather than immediately under the two links, so a thumb reaching for Support tickets is nowhere near it. The build string underneath is for support calls: it is the first thing an agent asks for.

Lanes, not a table
A table sorts; a kitchen triages. The three lanes are the three questions asked during service — what just came in, what is on the pass, what is waiting for a driver — and a card answers each one without being opened. There is no detail page to click into: everything the restaurant needs to cook is on the card.
Cards are not draggable. Status is a state machine, not an arrangement, and a card dropped in the wrong lane would be a write nobody meant to make.
One action per card
New carries Accept filled and Reject outlined in danger — deliberately unequal, because accepting is the overwhelmingly common act and rejecting costs a customer their dinner. The kitchen lane holds both Accepted (button: Start preparing) and Preparing (button: Mark ready for pickup), each card tagged with its state — the three manager transitions are exactly accept → preparing → ready. Ready carries no button at all, because the next move belongs to the driver, and the restaurant is told nothing about who is coming: it holds no deliveries:read, and its socket frame carries an order id and a status only.
Time since placed escalates
Neutral under 10 minutes, amber from 10, red from 20 — the only automatic colour on the screen, and it only ever appears on a card that someone is keeping waiting. On the Ready lane the clock restarts and reads “4 min ready”, since what matters there is how long the food has been sitting.
It ticks client-side once a minute from the placed-at timestamp, so it stays honest across a reconnect.
Keyboard first
Each lane is a list, each card a focus stop. ←→ move between lanes, ↑↓ between cards, Enter fires the card’s primary action and R opens Reject. ? lists the lot. Focus never moves on its own when a socket event arrives — a card appearing above the focused one must not steal the next Enter.

Why there are no buttons at all
Not a disabled Accept. A disabled primary invites clicking, and a manager mid-service will click it three times before reading anything. Removing it makes the card obviously not-yet-actionable and leaves the blue strip as the only thing to read.
Reject goes too: rejecting an order whose money is mid-flight is a race the restaurant should not be able to start.
Waiting, not broken
Blue, per the tone rule: something is in progress and moving. Not amber (nobody needs to act) and emphatically not red (nothing has failed). The card body steps back one notch in contrast so it recedes behind the actionable cards above it, while staying perfectly readable — the restaurant should still be able to start thinking about the food.
The copy names the actor: the bank. Not “processing”, not “please wait” — a manager who knows it is out of everyone’s hands stops looking for a button to press.
One exit is a frame, the other is a poll
The restaurant’s frame carries the order status only, never the payment status, so Authorized cannot arrive on the socket. While a card shows Authorising the dashboard re-reads that one order every 2 s; when it comes back Authorized the strip is replaced by the action row and the badge turns green — in place, no re-flash, because it is not new. On Failed the order goes Cancelled, which does arrive as a frame, and the card leaves the lane with a brief Order cancelled toast. If Accept is ever pressed in the race anyway, Orders.PaymentNotAuthorized puts the card straight back into this state rather than toasting an error.
If it sits in Authorizing past 90 s the strip gains a second line — “This is taking longer than usual” — and turns amber. Still no buttons; the restaurant simply knows to start the next order first.
Arrival, in full
The card enters at the top of the New lane and pushes the rest down — newest first, because the clock on an unanswered order is the thing being managed. Insertion is a 180 ms height-and-opacity transition; the cards below move with it rather than jumping.
The NEW flag and the accent ring hold for six seconds, then the card becomes ordinary. Six seconds is long enough to catch an eye returning to the screen and short enough that three arrivals in a minute do not leave the lane permanently lit.
Nothing scrolls, nothing takes focus, and no dialog opens. A manager typing in the reject modal when an order lands must not be interrupted — the counts update behind the dialog and the card is waiting when it closes.
The lane is an aria-live="polite" region announcing “New order #4835, 890 RSD” once. Polite, so it queues behind whatever the manager is doing rather than cutting across it.

Skeletons keep the lanes
Three columns, headers in place, two cards then one then one — the shape of a normal service, so nothing jumps when the data lands. The card skeleton includes its action-button block, because a card that grows a button after loading shifts every card below it.
Lane counts are blank rather than zero: showing “0” and then “3” is a worse lie than showing nothing. The whole region carries aria-busy and a polite “Loading orders”.
Empty is a result, not a void
A green tick, not a grey box: the restaurant has handled everything, which is the point of the screen. The one job left is to reassure — you can leave this open — and to prove the connection is alive, which the “Listening” pill does. A manager who cannot tell a quiet service from a dead socket will refresh every two minutes.
No illustration and no “Create order” button. There is nothing for the restaurant to do here, and inventing an action would be worse than the silence.
Error takes the whole panel
Not a toast over empty lanes. Three empty lanes and a dismissible message reads as “no orders” at a glance, and a restaurant would happily carry on cooking nothing. The panel replaces the lanes so there is no chance of misreading it.
The sentence that matters is the second one: orders placed while this is down are not lost. That is the fear. Retry is manual and automatic with a visible countdown, so nobody is left pressing a button that is already being pressed — and the error reference is there because the support agent will ask for it.

Reject an order

The only irreversible thing a manager can do from the dashboard, and the only place in this product where friction is the point. A reason is required, the order is terminal the moment it is sent, and the customer gets nothing back but a cancellation and a released hold — so the dialog shows exactly what they will see.

Pick a reason before rejecting
The confirm button is never disabled. Pressing it with nothing selected validates, moves focus to the group and says what is missing — a disabled button in a dialog leaves a manager staring at it with no explanation.
Red, and meant
Unlike the cart-conflict dialog on sheet 17, this confirm is red: it ends someone’s dinner and cannot be undone from either side. The order goes terminal the instant it is sent — there is no “undo” window, because the customer has already been told.
The safe choice is labelled Keep it, not Cancel: in a dialog about cancelling an order, a button marked Cancel is genuinely ambiguous.
Four reasons, one field
Radios, not a select: four options fit, and a manager under pressure should not have to open a menu to find out what the choices are. The set is short on purpose — a long taxonomy gets answered with whichever is first.
POST orders/{id}/reject takes one string, and the order the customer reads does not expose it. So the radio and the optional detail compose into that one reason (“An item is no longer available — out of kajmak this evening”), and the dialog says plainly that the customer will not read it. An apology to the customer, if wanted, belongs in a support reply, not here.
Showing the consequence
The preview panel is a compact copy of the customer’s terminal banner from sheet 23, badges included. A manager who can see Rejected · Released and “nothing is charged” knows what they are about to do without having to remember the payment rules.
It also quietly answers the question managers actually ask support: “will they be charged if I reject?”
Keyboard and focus
Opened with R on a focused card. Focus lands on the first radio, not the confirm; arrows move within the group; Tab is trapped in the dialog and Esc resolves to Keep it. On close, focus returns to the card’s Reject button — or, if the card has gone, to the lane heading.
There is no Enter shortcut for the confirm. Every other dialog in the product submits on Enter; this one does not, and that inconsistency is the point.

The toggle, three moments
0 ms
Flips on press. No spinner, no dimming, no waiting — the row is already dimmed because the item is now sold out.
~200 ms
Server agrees. Nothing happens visually — the success case is silent, which is the whole point of doing it optimistically.
fail
Rolled back to where it was, with a red ring for 2 s so the reversal is seen — plus the toast. A silent rollback is how a kitchen sells food it does not have.
Presses are queued per item and the last one wins; a manager flipping twice in a second never ends up fighting two in-flight requests. While a request is outstanding the toggle stays pressable — it is not disabled, because a kitchen correcting itself immediately is the normal case.
Why this one is optimistic
It is pressed constantly, by someone standing up, mid-service, often on a tablet on a shelf. A 400 ms wait per press turns a dozen flips into a screen that feels broken. The write is also trivially reversible and low-stakes compared with the alternative: an item shown as available for the two seconds it takes to confirm is a real order the kitchen cannot fill.
Nothing else on this screen is optimistic. Price edits, new items and category reorders all wait for the server, because none of them are pressed in a hurry and all of them are worse to get wrong.
The toast earns its place
Bottom right, red left edge, role="alert", and it names the item — “Couldn’t update” alone is useless when six rows were touched in a minute. It does not auto-dismiss under 6 s and carries Try again, which re-sends that one change.
Failures stack rather than replace: two failed flips means two toasts, because dropping one would leave an item silently wrong.
Categories are the customer’s order
The list is the running order of the menu, stated under it so nobody reorders by accident and wonders what changed. Rename is inline — click the name, it becomes an input, Enter saves and Escape reverts; there is no dialog for a four-character edit.
Reordering is a list of rows with up and down buttons — a FormArray, one group per category, swapping displayOrder — and Alt+↑↓ moves the focused category and announces its new position. There is no delete for a category or an item anywhere in the API; a mistyped item stays, and sold out is the closest thing to removing it.
Table by keyboard
One tab stop for the table, then ↑↓ between rows and ←→ between the controls in a row — forty items must not mean two hundred tab stops. Space flips availability from anywhere in the row, Enter opens the editor.
Each switch is a real role="switch" with aria-checked and a name that includes the item, so a screen reader hears “Ćevapi sold out”, not “switch, off”.

Validation & photo states
Name Give the item a name customers will recognise
Price RSD Price must be more than zero
Photo URL
This link didn’t load
You can still save — the item will simply show without a photo.
No URL yet — the preview stays an empty frame at the size the photo would occupy, so the drawer does not jump when one is pasted.
A URL is not an upload
The model stores a link, so the field is a link — no drop zone, no crop tool, no progress bar, none of which exist behind it. What the field owes the manager instead is proof: the preview fetches the URL as they type (debounced), reports whether it loaded, and states that the customer sees it cropped square.
A broken link is amber, not red, and does not block saving. The platform cannot tell a dead host from a slow one, and an item without a photo is perfectly valid.
Price is text, on purpose
A text input with inputmode="decimal", not type="number" — no spinner arrows to nudge a price by accident, no scroll-wheel edits, and no browser-specific formatting fights. The currency sits inside the field as a suffix so the number stays left-aligned with tabular figures.
Zero is rejected: free items are not a thing the order maths expects, and a mistyped price is far likelier. The value is normalised to a number with two decimals in one place and sent as the backend’s decimal; arithmetic is never done on it client-side.
Drawer, not a page
The table stays visible behind a light scrim, so the manager keeps their place and can see the row they are editing. New item opens the same drawer with the heading changed and the category pre-filled from whatever is selected in the list.
Closing with unsaved changes asks; closing with none just closes. Esc follows the same rule, ⌘S saves from any field, and focus returns to the row that was being edited.
No delete, and the form says why
There is no DELETE for an item or a category, so there is no delete button — a button that calls nothing is worse than none. For an item that is off tonight, or off for good, the availability switch in the table is the control. The missing endpoint is a known gap in the plan, not a design choice.
Edit sends name, description, price and photoUrl and nothing else, which is why category is shown as a fact on edit and availability lives in the table.

2 unsaved changes
Read-only is a different shape, not a grey field
A disabled input still looks like a field, so it reads as “editable, but not by you right now” and invites clicking. Commission and tax id are not fields at all: they sit in their own panel on a sunken surface, with a lock, rendered as display values in the type they deserve — 18.0% is a number the owner cares about, so it is set at 26 px, not hidden in a 13 px input.
The panel says who can change them and how. “Ask a platform administrator” is a route; a greyed-out box is a dead end. And it says the thing an owner actually wonders about the commission: the customer never sees it.
Coordinates come with a warning
Two raw decimal fields, monospaced, because that is what the model holds and pretending otherwise would need a map picker that does not exist. What makes them safe is the line underneath: drivers navigate to these, not to the address above. A manager who tidies up the street name and leaves the coordinates alone has done the right thing; one who nudges a digit sends every driver to the wrong block.
The save bar appears with the first edit
Nothing is sticky-saved and nothing autosaves — this page changes what customers see, so it waits. The bar arrives on the first change, counts what is pending, and offers Discard beside Save. Leaving with unsaved changes asks; leaving clean does not.
Validation runs on blur like everywhere else: email must be an address, phone is stored as typed, name cannot be empty. On save failure the bar turns amber and keeps the edits — a form that clears itself on a network error is a form nobody trusts twice.
Not on this page either
There is no opening-hours editor, no holiday closure, no preparation-time estimate, no delivery radius and no logo or cover photo upload — the restaurant model holds none of them. That is also why the customer-facing list on sheet 14 has no “open now” filter: the platform genuinely does not know.
The nearest thing a restaurant has to “we are closed” is rejecting incoming orders one by one, which is poor for everyone. If any single field were to be added to this model first, opening hours is the one to argue for.

Previous and next, nothing more
The customer’s list uses Load more; this one pages, because a manager reading a row aloud on the phone needs a stable position. But GET orders returns an array and no total, so there are no page numbers and no “of 128” — just the page you are on, a page-size choice, and Next, which disables itself when a page comes back shorter than pageSize.
Both badges, always
They get their own columns rather than sharing one, so the eye can scan a column of payment outcomes without reading the order states. Every pairing in this table is legal per sheet 08 — Cancelled · Failed, Rejected · Released, Delivered · Cash — and the column order puts the food before the money, matching every other surface.
No filters, because the API takes none
GET orders takes page and pageSize and nothing else — no status, no date range, no order number. A filter bar here would filter one page and look like it filtered the history, so there is none. A status or date filter on the endpoint is the first thing worth adding.
The page is sorted newest first. Finding “the order from Tuesday” means paging back — slow, and honest about why.
Dense, and drivable by keyboard
44 px rows, one tab stop for the table, ↑↓ to move, Enter to open an order, PgUp/PgDn to page. The order is the endpoint’s own, newest first — the other headers are not clickable rather than clickable-and-wrong.
No CSV export: no endpoint produces one, and a client-side export of the current 25 rows would be mistaken for the full period.
