The toggle is the screen
96 px tall and full width when offline, because going online is the only thing a stopped driver wants. Once online it shrinks to 72 px, loses its fill and moves to the bottom: still reachable, no longer the loudest thing, and nowhere near where a thumb rests while reading.
It is a real role="switch" with a label that states the action rather than the state — “Go online”, not “Online”. The current state is already carried by the badge at the top, which never scrolls away.
Busy has no screen of its own: a driver with a job is on sheet 38. The toggle is absent there, since going offline mid-delivery is not a thing the state machine allows — finishing the delivery is.
Two numbers, no money
Deliveries completed today and the time of the last drop-off — both derivable from the driver’s own delivery list, both genuinely useful to someone deciding whether to keep going. Set at 38 px because they are read at arm’s length.
There is no earnings figure, no payout balance and no shift planner, because the platform models none of them. A “today’s earnings” tile computed client-side from a per-delivery fee that does not exist would be the single most dangerous number in the product.
Permission denial is a full screen
Not a banner, not a toast. Without location the driver role does nothing at all, so the screen replaces the toggle entirely and spends its space on the only thing that helps: numbered, per-platform steps naming the exact labels on this phone. The Android copy differs (Settings → Apps → Trpeza → Permissions → Location) and is chosen from the user agent, not written generically to cover both.
Open settings deep-links where the OS allows it; I’ve turned it on re-requests rather than reloading, so a driver who fixed it in the background is back in two taps. If permission is still denied the screen stays and says so — it never silently returns to a home screen that cannot work.
The same screen covers “allowed once” and “while using” being revoked mid-shift: any transition to denied while online makes the app send PATCH delivery/drivers/me/availability { available: false } and land here — a driver who is Available but reporting no position is not an assignment candidate anyway, so staying online would be a lie.
Built for sun and gloves
Pure white surfaces, --text for body copy rather than the muted grey used elsewhere, and 2 px borders on secondary controls instead of 1 px — hairlines vanish outdoors. Nothing is smaller than 13 px, and nothing tappable is under 56 px.
There is no bottom tab bar anywhere in the driver app. One screen, one job; history and profile live behind the single menu button, which is the only chrome on the page.

Socket as the nudge, REST as the truth
GET delivery/drivers/me/offers is the authority: live offers only, soonest deadline first, lapsed ones excluded server-side. The DeliveryOffered frame carries just { deliveryId, orderId, offerExpiresOnUtc } and means “re-fetch the list” — the card is always built from the list, never from the frame, so a driver who was offline for the frame and one who received it see the same screen.
There is no retraction frame. An offer ends by lapsing, by being rejected, or by being accepted; the client self-expires on offerExpiresOnUtc and re-fetches. Losing the race is a 409, rendered as the expired state below. A new offer also buzzes the phone once.
One gap, prerequisite #5. The offer carries restaurantId and the pickup coordinates, not the restaurant’s name or street — and a driver holds no restaurants:read to look them up. Until a pickup name and address are added to the offer and to DeliveryResponse, the card shows a pin and the tagged name. Distances are straight-line from the driver’s own position; there is no routing.
The countdown is derived, never counted
The client shows offerExpiresOnUtc − now, recomputed each second against the device clock — not a 20-second timer started when the screen rendered. A frame that arrives two seconds late, a phone that slept, a reconnect mid-offer: all of them land on the right number, and an offer that is already gone opens directly in the expired state.
Tabular figures at 34 px, m:ss, so the digits do not shuffle sideways as they tick. The bar beneath it is the same value drawn wide, for a driver glancing rather than reading. Under prefers-reduced-motion the bar steps once per second instead of animating smoothly.
Two targets, deliberately unequal
Accept is 76 px and filled; Reject is 60 px and outlined, below it. Accepting is the common act and the one a driver will do while moving; rejecting can afford a deliberate reach. Neither confirms — both are recoverable in the sense that matters (a rejected offer goes to someone else; an accepted one can be finished only through the delivery’s own flow), and a confirm step inside a 20-second window is cruel.
Nothing else on the screen is tappable. No map, no phone numbers, no back arrow: at this moment the driver has exactly two choices and the screen offers exactly two.
Expiry is a state, not an error
Neutral grey, not red: nothing failed and the driver did nothing wrong. The copy says so outright, because a driver who thinks they were too slow starts tapping faster than they can read. The screen also confirms they are still online, which is the anxiety the moment actually creates.
The same screen covers the lost race — tapping Accept a fraction late gets this, with the wording unchanged. And it auto-returns to the waiting screen after ten seconds, so a driver who put the phone in a pocket comes back to the state that can receive the next offer.

One address is large; the other is a reminder
Heading to the restaurant, the restaurant is 27 px and the drop-off is a quiet “Then” card — useful for deciding a route, never competing for the glance. After pickup the two swap: the customer’s address takes the large type and the restaurant disappears entirely, because the driver is done with it.
The map shrinks in the second state (250 px → 196 px) to make room for the note. Nobody navigates from this map; it exists to orient, and the real navigation is one tap away.
The drop-off note is the loudest thing on the screen
Amber, 2 px border, 16 px bold body — heavier than the address above it. A note is only ever written when something is not obvious (a broken buzzer, a back entrance, a dog), and a driver who misses it makes a call the note existed to prevent. It is placed above the actions so it is read before anything is tapped, and it is never truncated: a long note grows the card and pushes the map, it does not get an ellipsis.
With no note the whole card is removed rather than shown empty, and the map keeps the space.
Delivered is the one confirm
Mark picked up fires immediately — a mistake there is annoying and fixable by carrying on. Mark delivered is terminal: it closes the delivery and moves the customer’s order to Delivered. (A card was already captured when the restaurant accepted.) A phone in a pocket against a jacket can fire a single 76 px button; it cannot fire two, in different places, in sequence.
So the sheet’s confirm sits above the dismiss and 200 px from where the original button was — a second tap in the same spot must not complete the action. It is green rather than accent: this is the good ending, and green here means “finished well”, consistent with the status legend on sheet 08.
A slide-to-confirm was considered and rejected: gloves and rain make dragging unreliable, and a control that sometimes does not respond is worse than one extra tap.
Payment is one line, and it matters
“Already paid by card” or “Collect 2 890 RSD in cash” — the second variant is accent-tinted and carries the figure at the same weight as the address, because collecting the wrong amount (or nothing) is the most expensive mistake available on this screen. Today the driver cannot know either: DeliveryResponse carries no payment method and no amount, and a driver cannot read the order. Prerequisite #6 adds both. It also appears in the confirm sheet, which is the last moment it can still be acted on.
Offline, both actions queue and replay in order on reconnect — a 409 on replay means the first attempt landed — and the button shows “Saved — will send when you’re back” rather than failing, per sheet 12. The delivery does not get stuck because a courtyard has no signal.

Trpeza Driver 1.0.0 · build 482
Three timestamps, side by side
Assigned, picked up, delivered — in a single row so the gaps between them are readable at a glance. That is the shape a driver checks when support asks “how long were you at the restaurant?”, and it needs no arithmetic on the screen to answer.
Deliberately not computed: no duration, no average, no distance total, no performance score. The platform stores three moments and nothing that judges them; a client-side “11 min” would quietly become a target nobody agreed to.
A stamp that never happened is an em dash in muted grey, not a blank or a zero — a cancelled delivery shows exactly how far it got.
Delivery status, not order status
The badge here comes from the delivery, not the order — the driver’s side of the job. Delivered green, Cancelled red, and a cancelled row steps back in contrast because there is nothing in it to act on. No payment badge anywhere in the driver app: how the customer paid is only the driver’s business at the door, and that line lives on sheet 38.
Two fields editable, one locked
PUT delivery/drivers/me takes firstName, lastName and vehicleType (the name, e.g. "Car"), so those are editable here; tapping the name opens the same small form. Email carries a lock glyph and a sentence, because it is the sign-in and no endpoint changes it.
Vehicle is the one that matters. It changes in the real world — a bike swapped for a car on a wet shift — and it is shown to the restaurant on the delivery. Change opens the same three radio cards as onboarding (sheet 54) and waits for the server; it is not optimistic.
Still no tab bar
These two screens reach each other and the home screen by a 48 px back arrow and one link — three destinations do not justify permanent navigation, and the bottom of a driver’s screen belongs to the primary action even when there isn’t one right now.
Log out is outlined in danger and sits below a spacer, the same pattern as the customer profile on sheet 27. An offer arriving while either screen is open replaces it: the offer always wins, and both of these screens are safe to be interrupted because neither holds unsaved input.

Page 1
Claim is one click, and only where it applies
An unassigned row carries a filled Claim button; an assigned one does not, because claiming someone else’s ticket is not a thing an agent should be able to do by reflex. The row menu holds Unassign (its reason is required) and Open. Assign to… appears only for an administrator, because naming someone else needs support-tickets:administer — and its picker has no roster to list (prerequisite #9).
Claim writes assignedAgent = me and nothing else — it does not move the ticket to In progress. Taking a ticket and starting work on it are different moments, and conflating them makes the status column useless.
Eight columns, ranked by scanning order
Reference first because it is what people quote on the phone; subject takes all the slack; priority and status sit together so the pair reads as one signal. Agent shows You in bold for your own tickets and an italic Unassigned in muted grey for the rest — the two things an agent scans for, made different in weight as well as colour.
Subject truncates with an ellipsis rather than wrapping: a fixed row height is what makes forty rows scannable, and the full text is one keystroke away.
Filters are server-side and in the URL
Status, category, agent, unassigned-only and the date range are the endpoint’s own parameters and all round-trip through the URL — there is no text search, so there is no search box — so a shift lead can send “unassigned payment issues, last 7 days” as a link. Active filters are tinted; Clear only appears when something is set.
Sorting is by opened-at, newest first, and that is the only sortable column — the endpoint orders by nothing else, so the other headers are inert rather than clickable-and-wrong.
Keyboard throughout
One tab stop for the table, then ↑↓ between rows and ←→ between a row’s controls. C claims the focused row, Enter opens it, / jumps to the filter bar and Esc returns from it.
The row menu is a real menu: arrows move within it, Escape closes it and focus goes back to the button that opened it. Rows never reorder under the focus ring — no frame announces a new ticket, so the queue re-reads every 30 s and on focus, and new rows wait in a “3 new tickets” pill above the table rather than inserting themselves. The customer column shows an id because the Support module keeps no customer names (prerequisite #7).

Two agents scanning the same queue will reach for the same ticket — it is the normal case at the start of a shift, not an edge case. The conflict has to resolve in a way that leaves nobody confused about who owns what, and without making the loser feel they did something wrong.

The row rewrites itself with the truth: Marko’s name, no Claim button. Amber tint for 3 s, then an ordinary row.
Marko V. took T-2291 first
It’s assigned to him now. Nothing you did went wrong.
Amber, not red
Nothing failed. The system worked exactly as designed and the ticket has an owner — it simply is not this agent. Red would train agents to read a normal race as a system fault, and after the third time they would stop reading it at all. The copy closes with the sentence that matters at the start of a busy shift: nothing you did went wrong.
The row is the real message
The toast can be missed; the row cannot. On a 409 — the claim lock lost the race — the client re-reads that one ticket with GET support/tickets/{id} and re-renders that row with the winner’s name and no Claim button, rather than refetching the whole page (a ProblemDetails body says who lost, not who won) — nothing else moves, and the agent’s place in a 25-row list is preserved. Open it is offered because the loser often still wants to read the ticket, and never assigns anything.
There is no ticket frame on the socket, so the queue’s 30-second refresh is the only other way a row learns it was taken: if the row already shows an owner, the button is simply gone and the press never happens.

Skeletons keep the filters real
The filter bar renders as actual disabled controls rather than grey blocks — it comes from the URL, not the response, so it is known before the data is. The table below is row-shaped, four rows deep, with the action column stubbed so nothing shifts when the buttons arrive.
Two different empties
Shown here is filtered to nothing — the filters stay visible above it, the copy names the filters in play, and the action clears them. The other case, a genuinely empty queue, gets the green tick and “No open tickets” instead, like the manager dashboard on sheet 30: one is a dead end to escape, the other is good news.
Telling them apart matters because an agent who sees the wrong one concludes support is broken, or that there is no work, and both are expensive mistakes.
Error replaces the table, keeps the filters
Same rule as the manager dashboard: a toast over an empty table reads as “no tickets”, and an agent would sit through a quiet hour that was actually an outage. The filter bar survives so a retry does not lose the agent’s place, retry is both manual and automatic with a visible countdown, and the error reference is printed because support-for-support will ask for it.

The header is facts, not decoration
Six meta fields in one row — customer, order, agent, and the three timestamps. The order number is shown as text, not a link: a support agent holds no orders:read, so there is no order screen to open — the ticket carries what the agent needs, and the refund dialog reads the subtotal cap from the ticket’s replicated order. Resolved shows an em dash until it happens; a missing timestamp is never a blank cell.
Status is a real <select> tinted to its current value, so the header shows the state and changes it in the same control. Most moves write immediately and land in the audit trail; Resolved and Escalated first open a one-line field, because the server requires a resolution note or a reason for those two. An illegal move comes back as a 409 whose detail is shown as it is.
Internal notes break the conversation shape
Customer and agent messages are bubbles on opposite sides with avatars. An internal note is none of those things: full width, square-ish corners, a dashed amber border, a 4 px amber spine, no avatar, no side — and a header that says in words that the customer cannot see it.
That is four independent signals (shape, position, colour, label), so the note still reads as internal in greyscale, at a glance, or to someone who has never used the product. Tinting an agent bubble a slightly different colour would not survive any of those tests.
System rows are neither
A refund request, a status change or an escalation appears as a centred pill in the thread — no bubble, no author avatar, because nobody said it. It keeps the chronology honest without competing with what people actually wrote, and the full record lives in the audit trail on sheet 44.
768: the header folds, the thread does not
The six meta fields collapse behind a Details disclosure and the subject line takes their place; status and refund stay on the surface because they are actions, not information. The thread keeps full-width bubbles at 82% and the composer keeps both mode buttons at full size — the mode switch is the last thing that should shrink on a narrow screen.
43 · Composer Composer.dc.html 2320 × 1780 px
43 · Support

The composer

The highest-stakes control in the product. Typing “third complaint this week, restaurant is a mess” and sending it to the customer is a one-keystroke mistake that cannot be recalled. So the two modes do not share a look: switching modes repaints the whole composer, and every part of it — border, fill, label, placeholder, button colour, button words — changes at once.

Reply to customer
default on every ticket
The customer gets this by email and in the app
⌘↵ to send
Internal note
the whole region repaints
INTERNAL NOTE — THE CUSTOMER WILL NOT SEE THIS
Visible to agents and administrators only
The switch itself
announced, not just repainted
Switched to internal note. Nothing you write now reaches the customer.
Note for the team…
Visible to agents and administrators only
The confirmation line sits inside the composer for 4 s and is an aria-live region, so the change is spoken as well as seen. The mode buttons carry a focus-style ring on the newly selected one — the switch reads as an event, not just a repaint.
Internal → reply, with text in the box
the only place this stops you

Send this to the customer?

You wrote this as an internal note. Switching to Reply keeps the text, and the customer will be able to read it.

Third complaint about Kod Gazde this week. Flagging to ops before we refund again.
Reply → internal never asks: moving text away from the customer is always safe. This asymmetry is the whole point — friction only in the direction that can leak.
Six things change, not one
Containerwhite, solid border → amber fill, 2 px dashed border
Bannera quiet line → a solid amber bar in caps
Placeholder“Write to the customer…” → “Note for the team…”
Field borderneutral → amber
Buttonaccent “Send to customer” → amber “Save internal note”
Verbsend → save — different actions, different words
Any one of these alone could be missed by a tired agent at the end of a shift. Together they make the mode unmistakable from across a desk, in greyscale, and in peripheral vision — which is when the mistake actually happens.
Why amber and not red
Writing an internal note is a normal, encouraged act — not an error and not dangerous. Red would make routine work feel like a warning and would collide with the genuinely destructive reds elsewhere (reject an order, cancel, delete). Amber is the product’s “pay attention” tone, and this is exactly that: proceed, but know where you are.
The same amber, dashed border and lock glyph are reused on the posted note in the thread (sheet 42), so the composer and the result look like the same thing. An agent learns the signal once.
Mode is sticky, but never inherited
After saving an internal note the composer stays in internal mode — agents usually write two or three in a row, and flipping back each time would be the thing that eventually gets ignored. The chrome keeps shouting, so staying is safe.
Opening a different ticket always resets to Reply to customer. Mode is never carried across tickets: an agent who left T-2291 in internal mode an hour ago must not find T-2305 silently armed — and the reverse, arriving in reply mode, is the safe default because the chrome for the dangerous mode is what is missing.
Drafts are kept per ticket and per mode, so a half-written reply is still there after a detour into a note.
Keyboard, and the one thing it will not do
⌘↵ submits whichever mode is active, and the hint text under the box names that mode’s verb so the shortcut is never ambiguous. The two mode buttons are a radio group: ←→ moves between them, and the group is the first stop when tabbing into the composer — you cannot reach the text area without passing the mode.
There is deliberately no shortcut that switches mode and sends, and no shortcut for internal mode alone. A single keystroke must never be able to change where text goes.

Append-only. Entries cannot be edited or deleted by anyone, including administrators.
9 entries · all times CET
One sentence per entry, always the same shape
Actor in bold, then the verb in muted grey, then the change as two real badges with an arrow between them. Reading the column of bold names answers “who touched this ticket” without reading anything else; reading the badge pairs answers “what state was it in when”.
Badges are the same components as everywhere else in the product, so Requested → Approved here looks exactly like the refund badges on sheet 08. An audit trail that invents its own vocabulary is one more thing to learn under pressure.
Reasons are quoted verbatim on their own line. Where an action has no reason field — claiming, replying — there is no line rather than an empty one.
Messages are logged, never copied
“Ana T. replied to the customer” records that a message exists and when. The body stays in the conversation tab. Duplicating message text here would double the storage of every ticket, make the trail unreadable at twenty messages, and put customer-visible and internal text side by side in one scroll — the exact adjacency sheet 43 works to prevent.
The internal-note entry says so explicitly, so nobody reads the absence as a gap in the record.
Newest first, absolute times
Reverse chronological, because the question is almost always “what just happened”. Times are absolute to the second with tabular figures — “2 hours ago” is useless when an agent is reconciling against a payment provider’s log. The timezone is stated once in the footer rather than on every row.
The trail is a tab, not a side panel: at 1440 a permanent third column would squeeze the thread to unreadable width, and the trail is consulted occasionally rather than watched. At 768 it stays a tab, unchanged.
System is an actor too
A refund settling, a payment failing, an order auto-cancelling — these have no human behind them, and the trail names System rather than attributing them to whoever was nearby. Being able to tell an automatic transition from a person’s decision is the whole reason this screen exists.
The entry carries actorName — nullable, so it falls back to the actor id — and no role. The verb does that job: “approved refund” can only have been an administrator, “requested refund” an agent.

An agent can ask; only an administrator can approve, and never the same person for their own request. The dialog’s job is to make the cap obvious, make the reason mandatory, and make the four-eyes rule impossible to misread as a bug when nothing happens afterwards.

The dialog

The Request refund button in the header disables while one is pending, so a second request cannot be stacked on the first. Its tooltip and accessible description say why: a refund is already awaiting approval.
In the thread
a system row, not a message
You requested a refund · 390 RSD · awaiting approval · 14:30
Jovana R. approved the refund · 390 RSD · 14:46
Both rows are visible to agents only. The customer is told about a refund when the agent writes to them, or when the money moves — never by an internal workflow step appearing in their app.
Rejected by the administrator
the agent finds out here
Refund request rejected
Rejected
Jovana R. · 14:52 · “Restaurant disputes the missing item — check the pickup photo first”
The cap is shown three ways
As a number beside the label, as a bar filling toward it, and as a percentage of the order. The bar is the one that does the work: an agent typing 1 800 sees it hit the end and turn red before they have finished reading the error. Full 1 440 is there because “refund the whole thing” is the commonest case and retyping a subtotal invites a typo.
The amount is 24 px and bold — it is the single most consequential value on the screen, and it should be readable from the next desk when a colleague is asked “does this look right to you?”
The client cap is a courtesy; the server enforces it again. Partial refunds against an order that already has one settled must net against the remaining balance, not the original subtotal — that is a backend rule this dialog assumes but cannot verify.
“You cannot approve your own” is stated before, not after
The four-eyes rule is in the dialog, in blue rather than amber — it is how the process works, not a warning. Saying it before submitting is what stops an agent from hunting for an Approve button afterwards and concluding the app is broken, and it sets the expectation they will pass to the customer: it needs an administrator’s approval.
It also says plainly that sending this moves no money. An agent who believes the refund is done will tell the customer so, and the customer will ring back in an hour.
The agent’s view has no approve or reject control anywhere — not disabled, absent. Those live in the administrator’s queue, and an agent who also holds the Administrator role sees them there, on someone else’s request, never on their own.
Pending is a state on the ticket, not a receipt
After submitting, the dialog closes and the ticket header grows a grey band carrying the amount, the Requested badge and who it is waiting on. Grey, because waiting is neutral — the same reasoning as Pending on an order.
No frame announces a decision, so the band re-reads the refund when the ticket is opened and every ~20 s while it stays Requested, then changes in place: green for approved, red for rejected with the administrator’s reason quoted. Rejection offers Request again rather than leaving the agent to rebuild the request from memory.
One required reason, in words
POST support/tickets/{id}/refund-requests takes { amount, reason } and the reason is free text, required by the aggregate. So it is one field, labelled with its reader — the administrator — because a good reason is the difference between a decision made in ten seconds and one that bounces back. The ticket’s category already says what kind of problem it was.
It never reaches the customer. Everything here is internal, and the customer learns about the refund from the agent’s reply on sheet 43 — written in the mode that says so.

Median is the headline, mean is the footnote
Response and resolution times are both shown, but the median is set larger and labelled in brand colour while the mean sits beside it in grey. One ticket that sat over a weekend drags the mean into fiction; the median says what a normal ticket actually felt like. Showing only the mean is how support teams end up arguing with their own dashboard.
The first-response tile states its own denominator — 124 of 155 have a first response. An average over an unstated subset is the most common way a dashboard lies by accident.
Two series, four differences
Opened and resolved differ by hue, by stroke (solid vs dashed), by marker (circle vs square) and by an explicit legend using those same marks. Print the sheet in greyscale, hand it to a deuteranope, or look at it on a phone in sunlight — it still reads.
Category bars are a single colour on purpose. They are ranked by length, and length already carries the whole message; giving each category its own hue would invent six more colours to memorise and imply meaning that is not there. The status chart is the opposite case — those colours are already the product’s status vocabulary from sheet 08, so the segmented bar reuses them and every segment is repeated as a labelled badge with an icon underneath.
Workload shows the gap, not a ranking
Assigned and resolved sit as two stacked bars per agent, hatched vs solid, so the useful thing — the difference between what someone took and what they finished — is a visible gap rather than a number to subtract. Agents are ordered by volume, but nothing is scored, ranked with a medal or coloured red for being slow. This is a staffing view, not a performance review.
Unassigned is a row here, separated by a dashed rule and tinted amber. Fifteen tickets belonging to nobody is the single most actionable number on the screen, and it would be invisible in a chart that only listed people.
The date range is one control, stated twice
Presets cover the three ranges anyone actually asks for; Custom opens a two-field picker. The resolved dates are printed next to the presets, always, so a screenshot of this dashboard carries its own window — a screenshot captioned “last 30 days” is worthless three weeks later.
The comparison figure (“vs 138 in the previous 30 days”) is the same window shifted back, computed from the same counts. The arrow is grey, not green or red: more tickets is not obviously bad and fewer is not obviously good, and colouring it would be the dashboard taking a position it cannot support.
What the backend does not carry
No SLA model, so nothing here is “within target” or breached — the times are just times. No customer satisfaction score, no reopen rate, no per-restaurant or per-city slice of tickets, no tag vocabulary beyond the fixed category enum, and no export. Every figure on this sheet is a count, a sum or a duration over rows that already exist.
Durations are nullable: a window in which nothing was resolved has no resolution time, and the tile shows — rather than 0, because 0 would mean “instant”. The workload panel reads byAgent, whose agentName is nullable too — an unprojected agent falls back to their id. Check its exact fields before building the assigned/resolved pair.

The layout never collapses
Both states keep every tile and every card in its normal place at its normal size. A dashboard that swaps itself for one big illustration teaches nothing about what it will become, and worse, it is indistinguishable from a dashboard that crashed. Here the shape of the answer is visible on day one; only the values are missing.
Zero renders as 0 in grey, not as a blank and not as an em dash. Zero is a real, known answer. The em dash is reserved for the different statement “we cannot compute this” — an average with no inputs, a comparison with no previous period.
Zeros are data, not absence
ticketsPerDay is gap-filled server-side: a day with nothing is a row of zeros, not a missing row, precisely so a chart does not draw a line across it. So the eleven quiet days sit on the baseline with small markers, and the three busy ones rise at the right. Filtering out the zero rows would turn a fortnight into a three-day chart and invent a trend.
Point labels are printed directly on the markers while the series is short. At fourteen days they come off — at three days there is room, and reading exact values off a three-point line is what people will actually do.
Thresholds, stated out loud
An average of two response times is noise dressed as a metric. Below five observations the tile shows the count instead of the average and says why in one line. Below that threshold the median alone is shown for resolution time, tagged with its sample size in amber — 4 tickets — so nobody quotes it in a meeting without knowing what it rests on.
All presets stay live — the client cannot know when the dataset began, and a 90-day window of mostly zeros is a true answer. The blue band explains the quiet rather than switching anything off.
Empty is not an error
Nothing on either state is amber or red, nothing offers a retry, and nothing apologises. The blue band is informational in the product’s own vocabulary — the same tone as any other “here is how this works” message. The error state for analytics, when a request genuinely fails, is the error pattern from sheet 41 and looks nothing like this.
The zero state carries exactly one action: a link to the ticket queue. Not “import data”, not “set up tracking” — there is nothing to set up, and implying otherwise would send someone looking for a settings page that does not exist.

One component, two widths
The rail and the panel are the same list with different column budgets. At 320 a row is one line — order, status, time; at 1440 it adds the restaurant. Both use the socket’s own status vocabulary from sheet 08, so Placed and the dashed DriverAssigned appear as they arrive, and nothing is translated into REST numbers.
A row shows the new status only. The frame carries no previous status and no actor, so there is no “from → to” and no “by whom” — inventing either from what the client happened to see earlier would be wrong the first time a frame is missed.
Quiet is a state, not an empty state
A stream with nothing in it for four minutes looks identical to a broken stream, and that ambiguity is the whole problem this state solves. The quiet panel states three things: the connection is up, when the last frame arrived, and when the connection last proved itself. Older events stay on screen under a heading rather than being cleared.
There is no animated pulse or “listening…” shimmer. An agent has this rail in peripheral vision for hours; anything that moves forever is something they learn to stop seeing.
A gap in the connection is a gap in the record
The hub persists nothing per frame and has no backfill. Rather than silently stitching the two halves together, the feed prints a dashed divider naming the exact window that was missed. A feed that quietly closes over a two-minute hole invites the conclusion “nothing happened”.
While disconnected, existing rows fade and the footer reads Frozen at 19:41:08. Amber, not red: an interrupted convenience feed is not an outage.
Pause belongs to the reader
Reading a row while the list shifts under the cursor is the classic live-feed failure. Pause holds the list and buffers arrivals; the panel also pauses itself when the reader scrolls away from the top, and offers a count to resume. The newest row carries a one-time brand tint — simply present, not animated, under reduced motion.
The rail is a reading surface only. An order id is text: an agent holds no orders:read, so there is no order screen to open, and acting from a stream that may be stale is how the wrong thing gets done.
What the frame carries, and what it does not
SupportActivity { orderId, restaurantId, status, occurredOnUtc }, pushed to the support group — every caller holding support:dashboard, which is SupportAgent only. An administrator does not receive it, so this screen is not in the admin area.
Prerequisite #8: the frame names the restaurant by id, and an agent cannot resolve it — no restaurants:read. Until a restaurantName rides on the frame, the column shows a short id. The restaurant and status filters work on what has already arrived, and say so.

Login

Email and password against an OAuth password grant, one button, one possible failure message. Everyone enters the product here — customer, manager, driver, agent, administrator — and the form has no idea which of those it is talking to until the token comes back.

375 · submitting
one request, one chance
F

Sign in

Order food, or get to your work account.
Checking your details
New here? Create an account
One failure, said once
The grant returns invalid_grant for a wrong password, an unknown email, and a disabled account alike, and the screen repeats that ambiguity exactly. There is no “we don’t recognise that email”, no green tick on a valid address, no different wording for a locked account — each of those turns the form into an oracle that tells a stranger which of your customers exist.
So the message sits above the form, not under a field, and neither field gets a red border. Marking one would be a hint by layout even with neutral words. Focus moves to the password field on failure — the likelier typo — without claiming that is where the error was.
Both values survive
The password is not cleared on failure. Clearing it is a habit inherited from shared terminals, and on a phone it costs the honest user — the overwhelming majority of people who see this message — a full retype of something they got almost right. Show remains available so they can look at it rather than guess again.
Submitting disables both fields and the button, so a double tap cannot fire a second grant request. There is no idempotency key here because there is nothing to make idempotent — a duplicate token request is wasteful, not dangerous — but a second attempt while the first is in flight makes the rate limiter, not the user, decide what happens next.
1440 · default
same form, centred — no marketing panel, there is no marketing
F

Sign in

Order food, or get to your work account.
New here? Create an account
Managers, drivers and support staff receive an invitation by email instead.
The same door for five roles
Nothing on this screen asks who you are. The grant returns a token carrying the roles, and the shell from sheet 11 decides what to show — a driver lands in the driver app, an agent in the queue, a person holding two roles in the area switcher. A role picker here would be a lie: the client cannot know the answer before the server does.
The one line about invitations is the only acknowledgement that staff accounts exist. It sits in small grey text because it matters to a handful of people and would otherwise confuse the thousands it does not apply to.
Nothing decorative
At 1440 the card is the same 420-wide form, centred on an empty page. The half-screen photograph is the default for a login page and it is dead weight here: it delays the first paint, it carries no information, and this product has no brand photography to put in it. The desktop layout is simply the phone layout with the page around it.
Autocomplete attributes are set properly (username, current-password) so password managers fill both fields in one action — the single largest speed-up available on this screen, and free.
No way back in
There is no password reset. No forgotten-password endpoint, no reset token, no email template — so this screen deliberately shows no “Forgot password?” link rather than linking to something that does not exist. Anyone who forgets their password today is locked out permanently and has to be dealt with by hand.
The machinery is nearly there: the invitation flow on sheet 51 already issues a single-use, expiring token by email and sets a password with it. A reset is that same token issued on request. Until it exists, this is the largest support cost hiding in the product.
Also absent: no social sign-in, no magic link, no two-factor, no “remember this device”. The lockout policy — five failures, fifteen minutes — is stated in the rejected state as a fact about the policy, never as a claim about this account, so it reveals nothing about which email exists.

One character short and still nothing is red — the counter is grey and the bar is neutral. Being told off mid-word is the thing this avoids.

Errors appear on the fields that caused them, after the field has been left or the form submitted — never while typing for the first time.
The rule arrives before the mistake
“At least 12 characters” is rendered under the password field on first paint, with an empty circle and a 0 / 12 counter. It is a checklist item, not an error, so it is grey. As characters go in, the counter and the bar move; when twelve is reached the circle fills green and the text stays put. Nothing turns red until submit, or until the field is left with something too short in it.
That is the whole design: the requirement occupies the same pixels whether it is unmet, met, or failed, so nothing jumps and the person is never surprised by a rule they had no way of knowing.
Five rules, no strength meter
Production Identity requires twelve characters plus the default character classes — an uppercase letter, a lowercase letter, a digit and a symbol (Development relaxes all of it to one character; the form validates against production either way). So the length gets a counter and a progress bar, and the four classes get small chips that tick as they are met. None of it is a strength score: a coloured meter would imply a judgement the server does not make.
Show/hide is present and defaults to hidden. A twelve-character minimum pushes people toward passphrases, and a passphrase that cannot be checked is a passphrase mistyped.

Customers only, silently
There is no role selector, no “are you a restaurant?” link, no driver recruitment banner and no partner enquiry form — not even in the footer. Self-registration produces exactly one role, and a screen that hints otherwise generates applications nobody can process and support tickets asking where the driver sign-up went.
The word “customer” never appears either. To the person filling this in there is only one kind of account, so naming the role would raise a question rather than answer one. The login screen carries the single line about invitations; this screen carries nothing.
Errors land on fields, not in a banner
Unlike login, registration failures are specific and actionable, so they are attached to the field that caused them and the field carries aria-invalid. A taken email gets a route out — Sign in instead — because the person is most likely someone who already registered and forgot.
This does confirm that an address is registered, which login refuses to do. That is unavoidable: a registration form cannot both prevent duplicates and hide whether they exist. The mitigation is that the message appears only after a full, rate-limited submission — never as you-type validation, which would turn the field into a fast address-checking oracle.
What the backend does not carry
No email verification. The address is stored and used for sign-in with nothing confirming it belongs to the person — so the screen makes no promise about a confirmation link, and after submitting, the customer is signed straight in. Whether that is acceptable is a product decision, not a design one, but it should be a deliberate decision.
Also absent: no phone number (there is no field for it and no SMS anywhere), no terms or privacy acceptance step, no marketing consent, no referral or promo code, and no delivery address at sign-up — the address is typed at checkout each time, per sheet 18. And because there is no password reset, the password chosen here is permanent in practice.

The link speaks first
Before any field, the screen states what it knows — which is exactly one thing: the email, read from the link’s query string along with the token. It is shown first so someone who was invited by mistake can recognise that and stop. The role, the name and the inviter are not in the link and no endpoint looks them up, so the screen does not guess at them.
The email is printed as a read-only fact, not a disabled input. A greyed-out field invites editing and implies the value is theirs to choose; it is not — the accept call must send the same email the invitation was issued to.
Three failures, three different pages
Expired, already used and unrecognised are genuinely different situations and each gets its own wording, icon and colour: amber for a timing problem, green for “this already worked, go and sign in”, neutral grey for a link that means nothing. Collapsing them into one “invalid token” page would send a person who already has an account looking for someone to re-invite them.
The expired and used pages name the email because the server recognised the token and can prove who it belongs to. The unrecognised page names nothing, for the same reason the login screen says nothing.

One step, not a wizard
The whole flow is a single screen and a single button labelled Set password and sign in, which is exactly what happens: two calls in a row — POST users/accept-invitation { email, token, newPassword } (204), then the ordinary password grant with the password just chosen — and the person lands in their area — a driver in the driver app, a manager on their dashboard. No confirmation page, no “now sign in with your new password”, no second trip through the login form.
There is no confirm-password field. It doubles the typing for everyone to catch a typo that Show already catches, and it is the wrong trade on a phone in a car park — which is where a driver will open this.
The same password rule, the same component
Twelve characters and the four character classes, shown from first paint — the identical block from sheet 50. A staff account has the same policy as a customer account, so it gets the same control, down to the pixels. Divergence here is how two password rules end up in one product.
The same block also means the same rule source: one validator, shared by registration and activation, written against the production rules rather than the relaxed development ones.
What the link carries, and what it does not
The link is /auth/activate?email=…&token=… (prerequisite #3 points the email at the SPA). The token is opaque, so the screen knows the email and nothing else — no role, no inviter, no expiry date. Showing those would need an invitation lookup endpoint; it is listed as a nice-to-have, not designed around.
The three failure pages need the accept call to answer with three different title codes for expired, already used and unknown. Verify what it returns; if it is one code, ship only the neutral “this link isn’t valid” page.
Absent: no self-service resend (nothing anonymous may cause an email to be sent), no way for the invitee to decline, no vehicle details for a driver — those are set later — and no administrator-side screen for creating or revoking invitations anywhere on this canvas yet. That screen is the missing other half of this flow.

The restaurant itself: who they are, where they are, how to reach them, and what the platform takes. Two steps, and the second one creates the person who will run it. Nothing here is editable later by the manager — commission and tax id in particular are set once, here, by an administrator.

What the platform keeps from each order. The manager can see it but never change it.

Entered as a percentage, stored as a fraction
You type
17.5 %
Sent and stored
commissionRate: 0.175
On a 2 400 RSD order

The conversion happens in the client, once, on submit. Everywhere the rate is read back — the restaurant profile on sheet 34, this form on re-entry — it is multiplied by 100 again and shown with the same % suffix, so nobody ever sees 0.175 in a field.
Guard, shown when it trips: “0.175 looks like a fraction. Did you mean 0.175 % (about two dinars on a 1 200 RSD order)?” — anything typed below 1 asks this once, because a fraction pasted into a percentage field is the one mistake on this screen that costs real money and nobody notices for a month.
Nothing is created until step 2 is submitted. You can still go back.
The unit is stated three ways
A percent suffix inside the field, a literal you type → stored pair showing 17.5 % becoming 0.175, and the money it means on a real order. The API’s unit is not a secret to be hidden behind a nice input; an administrator setting a commission will be asked to confirm it against a contract written in percentages and a database holding fractions, and this panel is what lets them do that without a calculator.
The field itself is right-aligned monospace with the suffix outside the text. Typing does not reformat under the cursor, and the panel updates on blur — live-converting each keystroke makes 1 flash as 0.01 on the way to 17.5, which is exactly the confusion this is meant to prevent.
The sub-one guard
Somebody will eventually paste 0.175 into this field because that is what the database holds and what the API docs show. The result is a restaurant billed at 0.175 % — a hundredfold error that produces plausible small numbers and survives review. So any value below 1 raises a one-time confirm that states the consequence in dinars rather than in percent.
It confirms rather than blocks: 0.5 % is a legitimate rate for a promotional deal, and a validator that refuses it would be wrong. The rule is “make the rare case deliberate”, not “make it impossible”.
Two steps, one creation
Step 1 does not write anything. The restaurant and its manager are created together when step 2 is submitted, because a restaurant with no manager is a dead record nobody can operate and there is no screen anywhere to attach one later. The footer says so, so an administrator who gets called away does not go looking for a half-made restaurant in the list.
Required fields are marked with an asterisk and validated on blur; errors follow the touched-only rule from sheet 18. Coordinates are the only optional pair, and the helper says exactly what is lost by skipping them rather than just calling them optional.
What the backend does not carry
No address lookup or geocoding — every line is typed and the coordinates, if wanted, are pasted from a map by hand. No opening hours, no delivery radius, no minimum order, no logo or cover image, no bank or payout details, no contract document, and no draft state for a half-finished restaurant.
Cuisine is one free-text string, not a list of tags and not an enum — so a place that is both a bakery and a grill has to pick one wording, and nothing keeps “Grill” and “grill” apart. The street and number are one field because the API has one street.

The button says what it does

This is the moment two records are written and an email leaves the building, and the label is the last chance to notice that the name in it is wrong. The blue panel above it states the same thing in a sentence, because sending mail to a stranger on someone’s behalf deserves to be announced before it happens, not after.
Step 1’s values are repeated as a compact review row with an Edit link. A wizard that hides the previous step behind a Back button makes people guess whether they typed the commission they meant.
The confirmation is a receipt, not a celebration
Three lines, each naming one thing that now exists or is in flight, with the third — the invitation — tinted amber because it is the only one that is not finished. The administrator’s job is done; the restaurant is not live in any meaningful sense until two other things happen, and the numbered list says which.
“No menu items yet” appears on the first line deliberately. A restaurant that customers can find with an empty menu is a bad first impression, and this is the only place anyone is told it will happen.
The typo is permanent

There is no invitation list, no resend, no way to change an account’s email, and no way to delete the orphaned account — so the confirmation says so in plain words rather than leaving an administrator clicking around looking for the button. The link expires eventually. There is no driver list to find him in later — keep the id this screen links to.
Onboard another driver View driver profile
Three radios, not a select
A fixed three-value enum with no default worth assuming belongs on screen, not behind a click. As cards they carry an icon and a line of context, they are one tab stop with arrow keys between them, and the chosen one is marked by border, fill, weight and the radio dot together — four signals, so it survives a bad screen.
Motorcycle is pre-selected as the common case and labelled “the usual choice” rather than silently checked, so the default is visibly a default and not a value the form invented.
One form, because there is one record
The restaurant flow is two steps because it creates two things that must exist together. A driver is one account, so this is one page with one button. Matching the two flows for consistency would add a step that does nothing except make the quicker job feel like the slower one.
Everything else is shared: the same blue “this sends an email” panel, the same verb-and-name button label, the same receipt with the outstanding item in amber.
What the backend does not carry
No phone number, no licence or document upload, no background check state, no vehicle details beyond the type, no zone or city assignment, no shift or availability schedule, and no pay rate — the driver pay model does not exist anywhere in the system, as sheet 39 already notes.
There is no driver list (GET delivery/drivers does not exist; one can be read by id), so the success screen links to the profile it just created and nothing else. An administrator cannot change a driver afterwards — the driver can change their own name and vehicle on sheet 39 — and nobody can deactivate a driver who stops working; they simply never go online again.

The rule is on the screen, not just in the API
A request the signed-in administrator made keeps its place in the list, tinted, with the buttons replaced by a padlocked chip reading Another administrator decides. Three weaker options were rejected: hiding the row (it looks lost, and nobody can tell whether it was ever filed), greying out live buttons (people click them and get a 403), and showing an error only after clicking (the rule should be learnable without failing at it).
The blue banner states the rule once, positively, in the product’s informational tone — it is how the process works, not a warning that someone did something wrong. The footer then says how much of the outstanding total is blocked on someone else, which is the one number this rule actually costs the team.
Everything needed to decide is in the row
Amount is the largest type on the line and right-aligned in tabular figures so the column scans as money. Next to it: the agent’s required free-text reason as one clamped line, the order, the ticket and who asked. An administrator should be able to decide most of these without opening anything — and the ticket reference is there for the ones where they cannot.
Rows are sorted oldest first within the tab, because a refund sitting unanswered is a customer waiting. The footer names the oldest wait rather than burying it in a column nobody sorts by.
Approve opens, Reject opens too
Neither decision fires from the row. Approve is labelled with an ellipsis — Approve… — the standard signal that a dialog follows, and its confirmation is sheet 56. Reject opens this dialog because the note is mandatory: a rejection with no stated reason is unanswerable when the agent, or the customer, asks why.
Reject is a secondary button with red text rather than a solid red one. It is not the dangerous action on this screen — approving is. The only solid red on the flow is the final confirm inside this dialog, where the decision is actually made.
What the backend does not carry
No approval limits by amount — every administrator can approve any sum, so the only control is that it is not their own request. No second approver above a threshold, no daily cap, no batch approve, no reassignment of a decision to a named administrator, and no notification to administrators that refunds are waiting: this queue has to be visited.
Also missing: nothing links a refund to the restaurant’s invoice, so a refund on a cold meal is the platform’s cost, never charged back. And the “third complaint this week” in that reason line was typed by an agent from memory — there is no per-customer or per-restaurant refund history anywhere to check it against.

3 · Sending
and the mismatch case below

Sending…

Recording the approval. The transfer itself is handed to the provider and settles separately.
Amount
1 440,00 RSD
to the card that paid order #4796
Mismatch — nothing shouts
Doesn’t match yet.
No red border, no error icon, no shake. A half-typed number is not a mistake — it is someone typing. The field only ever reports the positive: matched, or not yet.
Why typing, and not a hold or a timer
Hold-to-confirm and a three-second delay both make the action slower without making it more considered — you can hold a button down while thinking about lunch. Retyping the amount is the only friction that forces the eyes back onto the number that matters, which is precisely the value that must be right. It also catches the real failure mode here: approving the wrong row after scrolling.
Only the whole dinars are typed. Making someone enter 1440,00 tests punctuation, not attention, and a decimal separator that differs between keyboard layouts would produce failures that teach nothing.
The amount is said three times
38 px in tabular figures, spelled out in words underneath, and repeated inside the button label — Send 1 440,00 RSD, never “Confirm”. The words are there for the same reason a cheque carries them: 1 440 and 14 400 differ by one glyph and by a factor of ten.
The order’s subtotal sits beside the amount so a full refund is visibly a full refund, and a partial one visibly partial, without arithmetic.
Everything else points away from the button
Focus opens on the confirmation field, never on the confirm button, so a stray Enter or Space from the queue cannot carry through. Enter in the field does nothing until the value matches. Escape and Cancel both close with nothing sent. The confirm button is the only solid red in the flow and sits alone in the bottom-right, far from Cancel.
The green line restating that this is somebody else’s request is the last check on the four-eyes rule, at the moment it matters. The API enforces it too — this is a reminder, not the enforcement.
“Sending” means recorded, not settled
The in-flight copy is careful: the approval is being recorded, and the transfer settles separately. Saying “sending money” would promise an outcome this request does not have — what comes back is Approved, and Settled or Failed arrives later, on sheet 57.
The button is single-flight. If the response is lost, the dialog re-reads the request before offering a retry — an already-approved request comes back as a 409 whose detail says so, never as a second transfer.
A decision note, but optional here
Rejection demands a note; approval does not. Approving is agreeing with a case the agent already argued in writing, and forcing a sentence produces “ok” and “approved” in the audit trail — noise that makes the notes that do matter harder to find. An optional note field sits under the details for the cases where an administrator wants to say something.
The approval is logged regardless, with actor, amount and timestamp, per sheet 44.
No undo, and nowhere to cancel
Once approved, there is no endpoint to cancel or claw back a refund, and no screen that offers it. That is why the friction is here rather than in an “undo” toast — a five-second undo would be a lie about a transfer already handed to a provider.
The destination is the original payment: for a card order the provider refunds that card; the platform stores no card details an administrator can see, so the dialog names the order, not the card. A cash order has nothing to refund to — it ends Failed with a reason saying it must be settled by hand (sheet 57).

A failed refund, opened
what an administrator can actually do
640 RSD has to be settled by hand

The sequence
Marko V. requested 640 RSD
Yesterday 17:44:02
Ana T. approved it
Yesterday 18:02:11
System recorded the failure — Cash on delivery order; settle manually
Yesterday 18:04:53 · 2 min 42 s after approval
What happens now
There is no retry. A failed refund is final as a record. A cash order is settled outside the platform; a request that failed for its amount gets a new, smaller request from the agent. Either way it is a conversation, not a button.
Open T-2279 and tell the customer
The ticket carries the failure as a system row already, so the agent who asked for the refund sees it without being told.
The waiting row shows the question, not a spinner
An approved refund renders as the badge it actually has, then an arrow, then a dashed outline reading Settled? — the shape of the answer that has not arrived. A spinner would say “the page is loading”, which is false; the page is fine and the bank is slow. The line underneath gives the honest expectation: usually under a minute, sometimes a few.
Rows update in place when the outcome lands. No reordering, no jump, no toast — an administrator watching the list sees one badge replace another, and one who walked away finds the finished state when they come back.
Stuck is its own state
A refund still Approved after a threshold stops looking patient and turns amber: still, after 4 minutes. It has not failed — the system genuinely does not know — and inventing a Failed state the backend never sent would be worse than saying so. Amber, because it needs a human to go and look somewhere else.
The row says where: the provider’s own dashboard. Pointing outside the product is honest when the product has nothing to offer.
A failure names a cause, in plain words first
The response carries failedOnUtc and a bounded failureReason. The heading is ours, in plain words, chosen from the commonest causes (“Cash order — nothing to refund to”); the reason underneath is the server’s, verbatim, in smaller type. The heading is for the administrator deciding what to do; the raw reason is for whoever follows it up.
“No money left the account” is stated explicitly. The first question anyone asks about a failed refund is whether it half-happened. A Failed row with a reason is a call to action, not an alarm — red for the badge, but the panel’s job is the next step.
No retry, and no alternative payout
There is no endpoint to retry a failed refund, and no way to pay a customer by any route other than the original card — no bank transfer, no credit on the account, no voucher, because none of those exist in the data model. So the only action offered is opening the ticket, and the panel says why rather than showing a Retry button that would 404.
Also absent: no alerting when a refund fails (somebody has to be looking at this screen), no timeout that moves a stuck refund to a terminal state, and no reconciliation view against the provider’s ledger. The failure count on the analytics sheet is the closest thing to a signal, and it is a number on a dashboard nobody watches at night.

Ticket queue Support analytics Refunds · 6
Numbers on this page are read once when it loads: list lengths capped at 100, and one analytics call. They do not refresh on their own — reload to see them move.
Every tile is a filtered list
There is no metrics API and no list returns a total, so a tile is one of two things: the length of a list the API can filter (support/tickets?status=Open&unassigned=true, support/refund-requests?status=Requested, at pageSize=100, shown as “100+” when full), or a field of support/analytics/summary. Orders and deliveries get no tiles: their lists take no filters, so counting “in flight” would mean paging through all of them.
That constraint still produces a useful page. The work tiles are clickable and land on exactly the list they counted, so a number is never a dead end.
Only two tiles are coloured
Unassigned tickets and refunds awaiting decision carry a tint, because they are the two things on this page that are waiting on a person and will not resolve themselves. Tickets opened and resolved are just weather — a healthy platform always has some, and colouring them would make the page permanently alarmed.
The second row is context rather than work: restaurants (one page counted), and the analytics summary’s refund figures for the week — settled, approved but not yet settled, failed. The last two are the closest thing the platform has to a health check.
Stale by design, and it says so
The counts are read once at load and do not poll. The footer states that plainly rather than implying a live dashboard — the live surface is the activity feed on sheet 48, and this page links to it instead of pretending to be it. Polling eight endpoints on a timer to keep a landing page warm is cost with no reader.
No user management, anywhere
There is no user list, no search by email, no deactivate, no impersonation and no password reset on anyone’s behalf. PUT users/{userId}/roles exists, but with no list to find a userId there is no screen to put it on. Accounts come into existence through the two onboarding forms and cannot be altered afterwards by any screen in this product. The sidebar has no Users entry, because a nav item leading to a page that cannot do the obvious thing is worse than no nav item.
The consequences to plan for: a driver who leaves keeps a working account, a manager who changes email keeps the old one, a compromised account cannot be locked, and nobody can see who holds the Administrator role. Also absent: revenue, commission earned, payout runs, per-restaurant performance, and any platform-wide figure beyond these counts.

59 · System

Error taxonomy

Every failure from the API arrives in the same shape — RFC 7807 ProblemDetails, where title is a machine code the client branches on (Orders.MenuItemNotAvailable) and detail is the sentence a person reads. One payload, four places it can land. Which one is not a judgement call: it follows from where the user was and whether the page still works.

What the API sends
{
  "type":     "…",
  "title":    "Orders.MenuItemNotAvailable",
  "status":   400,
  "detail":   "Pljeskavica is no longer available.",
  "instance": "/orders"
}
// a ValidationError adds the field map:
  "errors": {
    "deliveryAddress.postalCode": ["Must be five digits."]
  }
title
the error code — the client branches on it (which cart line, which page, retry or not) and never renders it
detail
the human sentence — rendered verbatim, never parsed for meaning
errors
field pointers → the field-level surface, one message per input
status
400 Validation or Problem · 404 NotFound · 409 Conflict — plus the gateway’s 401/403/429
type
never shown to anyone; it goes in the console and the bug report

Only when the screen has nothing to show. Carries the response’s X-Correlation-Id as a reference an agent can find in Seq — never a stack trace.
Toast

For actions that failed while the page kept working. Bottom right on desktop, above the nav on a phone; errors stay until dismissed. Never for anything the user must act on.
Two that need their own wording
403 — permission denied
You don’t have access to this
Refund decisions are for administrators. Your account is a Support Agent, which can request a refund but not approve one.
Back to the ticket queue
If you think you should have access, ask an administrator.
Names the role that can do it and the role the user has. No status code, no type URI, no “Forbidden”, nothing that reads like a server talking.
429 — rate limited
Slow down a moment
Too many requests. Loading the rest in 4 s…
Never a countdown at checkout. The gateway sheds reads first (RateLimitTier.Read), so browsing meets this banner long before a write does. If placing an order, approving a refund or confirming a delivery is ever limited, it gets the inline form error with a manual retry instead — a countdown on a payment is unbearable.
The countdown comes from Retry-After, and the request retries itself when it reaches zero. No button, because there is nothing useful for a person to do.
All six, dark
subtle fills darken, text lightens, borders keep their job
Inline
Your cart has changed
Pljeskavica is no longer available.
Field-level
Must be five digits.
Full page
We couldn’t load your orders
Nothing was lost — try again.
Toast
Couldn’t change availability
Pljeskavica is back to Available.
403
You don’t have access to this
Refund decisions are for administrators.
429
Slow down a moment
Loading the rest in 4 s…
The code is for the client, the sentence is for the person
title is a code — Orders.PaymentNotAuthorized, Restaurants.NotFound — so the client branches on it: which cart line to mark, whether to offer a retry, which page to show. detail is prose written for people and is rendered verbatim. Parsing detail for meaning is the beginner mistake; a per-status table of friendlier phrasings is the other one, and produces “Something went wrong” for a message that said exactly what was wrong.
The client supplies only what the payload cannot: a heading keyed on the code where one helps (“Your cart has changed”), the retry, and the correlation reference. title, type and status are never rendered — they go to the console and to whatever the reference code looks up.
The rule is about the page, not the status
One question decides the surface: does the person still have a working screen? If the screen has nothing to show, it becomes the error. If the screen works and the failure was theirs to fix, the message goes where they were looking — the field, or the top of the form. If the screen works and the failure was incidental, it is a toast.
That is why 403 appears twice in the table. Opening a whole area you lack is a page; being refused one button is a toast. Same status, different amount of the screen destroyed.
Toasts never carry the only copy
A toast disappears, so nothing lives only in one: never a validation message, never a failed payment, never anything with a decision attached. The one place a toast is the whole story is the optimistic rollback on sheet 32, where the state on screen has already corrected itself and the toast merely explains why it moved.
Success and info dismiss after 5 s, errors stay until dismissed (sheet 06), stacked bottom right — above the nav on a phone — and announced through role="status" rather than alert — it should not interrupt a screen reader mid-sentence.
Colour is never the message
Every surface carries an icon and words; red and amber only reinforce. In dark mode the subtle fills drop to the dark ramp from sheet 01 and the text colour becomes the light variant of the same semantic, so the danger red on #2C1212 keeps the same contrast relationship it has on #FEF0F0. Borders do not lighten — they are what separates a tinted panel from the page when the fill is nearly black.
What this assumes
That title codes stay stable, and that detail really is written for people on every endpoint. A single detail reading Object reference not set to an instance of an object puts a stack trace in front of a customer, and no client-side rule can catch that. It is worth a test that fails on any detail containing a type name.
Also assumed: that errors keys match the client’s field names closely enough to map (unmapped pointers fall back to the inline surface rather than being dropped), and that 429 responses always carry Retry-After — without it the countdown has nothing to count and degrades to a plain message with a manual retry.
There is no localisation anywhere in the product, so the server’s language is the only language.

A skeleton is a promise about layout
The boxes sit exactly where the real content will, at the real sizes, in the real number — six table rows because that is the page size the view requests, three list cards because three fit above the fold. When the data lands, nothing reflows and nothing jumps under a thumb that is already moving toward a row.
Grey blocks with the opacity pulse from sheet 07 (1 → 0.45 over 1.6 s — Tailwind’s animate-pulse is close enough) and never a sweeping gradient; under prefers-reduced-motion the blocks hold still at 0.7. The container carries aria-busy and a label, so a screen reader hears “loading restaurants” rather than a hedge of empty boxes.
Skeleton once, then never again
Skeletons are for a screen that has nothing yet. Every later fetch — a filter change, a page, a lane refresh — keeps the old content on screen at reduced opacity with a small Updating marker in the section header. Replacing a table you were reading with its own skeleton is a worse regression than the wait it is trying to explain.
A full-page overlay spinner appears exactly nowhere after first paint. On a page that still works, it takes away everything that works.
Spinners belong to the thing that started them
An action’s wait is shown inside its own button, which keeps its exact width so the row does not twitch, changes its label to a verb in progress, and disables itself against a double submit. Everything else on the page stays live — a manager waiting on one accept can still read the next order.
Success is shown by the thing that changed, not by a toast. The row becomes Claimed by you; the order moves to the next lane. A toast confirming something already visible is one more thing to dismiss.
Why exactly one optimistic control
Three things have to be true together, and only the availability toggle has all three: it is used constantly under time pressure, the wrong state costs little for the seconds it lasts, and it is trivially reversible — the correction is the toggle flipping back. Compare accepting an order: used once per order, the wrong state has a kitchen cooking, and there is no undo.
Claiming a ticket fails the test on a different axis. It is quick and low-stakes, but it can genuinely lose — another agent claims it first — and an optimistic claim would show a ticket as yours before snatching it away. The rule is not “low stakes go optimistic”; it is “no realistic conflict, and a cheap rollback”.
The rollback speaks in the present tense
“Pljeskavica is back to Available” — the state now, not the verb that failed. A manager glancing at a toast mid-service needs to know what customers can currently order, and “Update failed” does not answer that.
The toggle takes one red ring as it returns so the eye catches the reversal even if the toast is missed, and the ring fades — or simply is not drawn — under reduced motion. Rapid taps collapse to the last intent: one request in flight, later taps queued, and only the final server answer decides the resting state.
